articles.title: Greenpeace activists create ‘boulder barrier’ in North Sea to deter industrial fishing
articles.summary:
Action taken to prevent bottom trawling in the marine protected area and conserve porpoise populations

Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of…

blocks.text: Greenpeace activists have dropped boulders in the North Sea to snag the dragnets of industrial trawlers fishing in a marine protected area.

Activists onboard the Greenpeace ship Arctic Sunrise dropped the giant stones to form an underwater barrier around the Southern North Sea marine protected area (MPA) – the UK’s most bottom-trawled MPA.

blocks.caption: Boulders were loaded on to the Arctic Sunrise in Le Havre.  Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace

blocks.text: The Southern North Sea is an area of importance for harbour porpoises, supporting nearly 20% of the UK North Sea population. But despite its MPA status, there are no restrictions on fishing in most of it. Bottom trawlers, dredgers and other industrial fishing vessels scour it daily.
Bottom trawlers logged more than 37,200 fishing hours in the protected zone in 2025, an act akin to “a bulldozer tearing through a treasured national park”, Greenpeace UK said.

blocks.caption: Greenpeace campaigners drop boulders onto the seabed to create anti-trawler barrier

blocks.text: “Hulking great ships prowl the sea day after day, stripping it of fish and killing precious wildlife like porpoises, sharks and sea birds,” said Will McCallum, the campaign organisation’s co-executive director. “With our ship and a movement behind us, we’re doing what the government isn’t: protecting our seas.”

The “boulder barrier” had effectively closed 116 sq km (about 45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea MPA to bottom trawling, Greenpeace UK said. Over the coming days, the Arctic Sunrise will patrol the area to deter any other kinds of industrial fishing. The activists have declared the zone an “ocean park”, in the spirit of Britain’s national parks.

blocks.caption: Greenpeace campaigner explains the "boulder barrier" on the seabed

blocks.text: The Southern North Sea MPA lies along the east coast of England, from north of Dogger Bank to the strait of Dover in the south. It is intended to protect porpoise populations, partly by ensuring the “availability of prey is maintained”. Greenpeace UK’s activists say intensive fishing in the area contradicts this objective.
“We announced in June that if the government didn’t act soon, Greenpeace UK would take direct action,” McCallum said.

blocks.caption: The boulders form an underwater barrier to prevent bottom-trawling fishing in the ‘ocean park’ zone. Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace

blocks.text: The action coincided with the nationwide premiere of Blue Planet III, the latest BBC wildlife documentary narrated by David Attenborough to focus on the oceans and the human-made threats they face. In 2025 bottom trawlers and dredgers tore through a cumulative 55,600 sq km of MPA seabeds, an area 58 times the size of Dartmoor national park, according to a Greenpeace analysis.
after newsletter promotion

blocks.caption: ‘We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries,’ said Kerry McCarthy, an MP and former climate minister who has supported the campaign.  Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace

blocks.text: A number of notable figures added their names to boulders tipped from the Arctic Sunrise into the North Sea. Among them was the Labour MP Kerry McCarthy, a former climate minister and a member of the all-party parliamentary group for the ocean, who said: “Industrialised fishing is having a hugely destructive impact on our marine environment, yet less than 1% of our seas are protected from it.

“[Fishing boats] can legally tear through supposedly protected areas of the ocean, wreaking havoc upon the seabed, precious habitats and the sea life that lives there. Progress is too slow and nature can’t wait, which is why I’ve added my name to one of Greenpeace UK’s boulders. We need a ban on bottom trawling and properly protected ocean sanctuaries, both here in UK waters and right across the Atlantic Ocean.”
The government has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Unions gain access to thousands of Google workers after UK employment rights overhaul
articles.summary:
Prospect to hold workplace sessions and recruit members under agreement with tech company

Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights…

blocks.text: Trade unions are expected to make further inroads into big tech companies in the UK after new rights for unions to access workplaces came into force, with Google UK signing an agreement on Monday.
The Prospect union has reached an agreement with Google to begin organising among about 7,000 workers across its UK operations, including YouTube but excluding DeepMind.

Google DeepMind is expected to strike a separate agreement, with the Communication Workers Union seeking recognition there. The deal follows a similar agreement between Prospect and Meta, which owns Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram and employs about 5,000 people in the UK.
The agreements will allow unions to communicate with non-unionised workers and encourage them to join.

The union, which represents more than 160,000 UK workers across several sectors, will now be able to run sessions inside Google’s workplaces, including the flagship headquarters in King’s Cross, London.

Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, said: “Prospect has been organising tech workers for many years, and this access agreement is a powerful signal of intent that we can successfully negotiate agreements with even the biggest global tech companies.

“Tech workers deserve a stronger voice at work, whether that is over bread-and-butter trade union issues like pay and flexibility, AI deployment or workplace culture. I am pleased that Google has struck this agreement with us, and hope it sends a clear signal to other tech companies that having a relationship with trade unions is the new normal in the sector.”

He said workers would have a stronger voice as more employees at Google and Meta joined trade unions. “With our track record of delivering wins for members, I am looking forward to seeing what we can achieve together.”
Google said it had signed the access agreement to comply with the new UK workplace legislation, although it maintained that it already had good internal employee relations.

“This step builds on our established work with internal employee representative groups, allowing us to fulfil these new requirements while preserving the respectful, direct dialogue our culture is built on,” a spokesperson said.
after newsletter promotion

Paul Nowak, the TUC general secretary, said last week that he expected a wave of union recognition deals in the private sector over the next year as the “transformative” rules on accessing workplaces came into force.

The Employment Rights Act gives unions the right to enter workplaces to meet workers or communicate with them electronically. From January, employers will be required to inform workers of their right to join a union.

Previously, unions seeking recognition have sometimes had to organise workers from outside their workplaces – as was the case with the GMB’s thwarted effort to gain recognition at Amazon’s warehouse near Coventry two years ago.

articles.title: ‘Politics of electricity’ over rising bills could power Democratic win, say clean energy advocates
articles.summary:
Concerns about datacenters and high energy bills could help Democrats clinch races in Ohio, Arizona and Michigan

In Arizona, where summer temperatures regularly hit triple digits, air…

blocks.text: In Arizona, where summer temperatures regularly hit triple digits, air conditioning can be a matter of life and death. This year, as the state recorded its hottest summer on record, Diali Avila’s monthly power bill went up to $400, the highest it has ever been.

Avila, the state director for Climate Power, an advocacy group, said the upcoming elections offered voters an opportunity to elect candidates who can ease their utility bills. “People are making the connection: they’re looking at their electricity bills that they get at the end of the month, and then they’re looking at their ballot, and they’re [realizing], this is my moment to take action,” she said.

Avila is among several clean energy and consumer advocates who say soaring bills such as hers – along with broader questions about affordability – could help move votes in November, as Democrats across the country seek to retake control of Congress.

“This midterm election cycle has the potential to become the first election cycle where electricity and utility bills become a top tier national political issue,” said Charles Hua, founder and executive director of PowerLines, a national non-partisan non-profit that aims to modernize utility regulations. “We’re entering a new politics of electricity.”

National average electricity prices have increased about 10%, in the last two years, according to federal figures, and a recent Pew survey found 74% of Americans said they were “very concerned” about gas and energy prices. A new poll from left-leaning Hart Research found that voters in battleground districts ranked utility bills among the three most important issues in the upcoming midterms.

The cost of energy has always been a political issue in America, but historically it has focused on the gas pump, said Hua. However, in recent years energy demands from datacenters, an ageing grid in need of repairs, climate emergencies such as wildfires and hurricanes that further weaken the grid, and the war in Ukraine has pushed up electric bills. (The war in Iran, meanwhile, has raised the price of gas).

Power bills are one part of a broader concern about affordability that has dominated this midterm cycle, said Geoffrey Henderson, who has researched candidate messaging on climate and energy this election.

“Utility bills were already on people’s minds in prior election cycles, but what’s changed is that datacenters are being proposed and advanced at such a fast rate, and there’s been so much community-level opposition to the datacenters that I think it’s elevating the utility bill question,” Henderson said.
In several races, Democrats are tying their opponents to those high utility bills and datacenters.
Ohio

In Ohio, which has the fourth highest number of datacenters of any state, Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate for Senate, has run ads calling Jon Husted, his incumbent, Republican opponent, the “face of datacenters”, connecting his support for the industry to rising electricity bills.

Electricity rates have gone up by 34% in Ohio since 2022, according to state figures, and a new poll from Ohio Northern University found 55% of Ohio residents oppose datacenter construction; 79% believe datacenters will drive up water and electricity costs.

Husted served as lieutenant governor in an administration that offered tax breaks to bring datacenters to the state, but in July, introduced a bill he said would help prevent utilities from shifting datacenter costs on to ratepayers; Senate Democrats blocked the bill, calling it “toothless”. In a leaked memo from 18 August, Republican strategists acknowledged: “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck.”

“This is an issue that has legs in rural Ohio, and I think it’s going to really help [Brown] close the margin in some of those Republican areas,” said Spencer Dirrig, vice-president of government affairs for the Ohio Environmental Council Action Fund Pac, which backs more regulations on datacenters. “That could be the difference in the election.”

In the state’s tight race for governor, both candidates – Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy – say they would support halting new datacenters until new regulations come into effect. Acton has criticized Ramaswamy for holding investments in the datacenter-related industry, calling it a conflict of interest; Ramaswamy has said he would divest if elected. (Acton herself held stock in companies tied to datacenters, but her campaign says she sold off individual stocks earlier this year to avoid conflicts of interest).

Acton has also said she would appoint commissioners to state utilities who would focus on lowering consumer costs, a move Dirrig says could have a real impact on Ohioans’ wallets. “If you want the clearest possible connection between your vote and your energy bill, it’s who you elect to be governor and who they appoint to be the public utilities chair,” he said. Ramawasmy has not publicly said who he would appoint, and his campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Michigan

In Michigan, the Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed has sought to tie his opponent, Mike Rogers to DTE Energy, the state’s unpopular, large private utility. El-Sayed has gone after Rogers for accepting donations from the company, which has been criticized for rate hikes and frequent outages as it signs contracts with datacenters. DTE did not respond to a request for comment.

A statewide ballot measure would ban regulated utilities such as DTE Energy from contributing to politicians; El-Sayed has said he supports the measure, while Rogers has not taken a public stance. Rogers did not respond to a request for comment.

“[El-Sayed] has done a good job of making himself an anti-DTE candidate,” said Brian Geiringer, executive director of Ann Arbor for Public Power, which is advocating for replacing DTE with a public utility. “He often names DTE explicitly.”

In Ann Arbor, a ballot measure proposes replacing DTE Energy altogether with a public utility; the city’s mayor and city council have opposed the measure. Despite these headwinds, Geiringer said the measure touches on a resonant theme this election season. “Paying your monthly bill and having your power go out in DTE territory all the time certainly is one of the most salient [examples] of corporations taking your money.”
Arizona

In Arizona’s sixth congressional district, which covers suburban Tucson, advocacy groups have run ads against the incumbent Republican Juan Ciscomani, saying his vote for the One Big Beautiful Act would increase residents’ utility bills by more than $200 a year and cut clean energy production. (The $200 figure is based on an estimate from the left-leaning Center for American Progress.)

Democrat JoAnna Mendoza, who is seeking to unseat Ciscomani, supports investments in clean energy and says her “top concern” is that constituents have the ability to pay for energy to cool their homes. In October, the Cook Political Report shifted its outlook on the race from “toss-up” to “leans Democratic”.

Starting in 2024, Ciscomani signed letters asking his party leadership to keep some Biden-era clean energy tax credits, but ultimately he voted for legislation that phased them out. (Ciscomani has defended his vote, pointing to compromises that he said would lessen the blow to wind and solar energies).

Since then, hundreds of workers were laid off at an EV factory in his district, and several clean energy projects have been cancelled in Arizona, which could have helped supply energy in periods of high demand, Avila said. “[Ciscomani’s vote] is really affecting not only electricity prices, but also people’s livelihoods and jobs,” she added.

Avila said she hoped that if Mendoza wins, she would push legislation to support the state’s clean energy industry. But she added that another state election might have more power to lower Arizonans’ utility bills in the near term: two of five seats on Arizona’s public utilities commission are up for grabs. Republicans have held a majority on the board for decades, and currently all five members are Republicans. “Democrats have an opportunity to rally this energy around electricity costs and flip two seats this November,” Avila said.

articles.title: Mamdani threatens ICE with legal action over use of New York parking lots
articles.summary:
Letter from mayor tells federal agents to stay out of city-owned facilities for immigration operations

Mayor Zohran Mamdani has threatened to take legal action against Immigration and…

blocks.text: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has threatened to take legal action against Immigration and Customs Enforcement over allegations the agency’s officers at the agency are using parking lots owned by New York City for operations in the area.

In a letter to the Trump administration, Mamdani noted the agency’s use of property owned by the city was “unauthorized and is therefore illegal, endangers City residents, and sows fear among those who seek to access City property”.
He added, “if your agents continue any unauthorized use of these lots, New York City will take legal action to prevent this unlawful commandeering of City property.”

The letter called on the Department of Homeland Security and other ICE officials to issue guidance immediately to ICE agents that stipulate they are prohibited from using any New York City parking lots to stage or conduct operations.
New York City has been a sanctuary city for immigrants since Mayor Ed Koch’s administration in 1989.

The Mamdani administration has criticized the Trump administration over ICE activity in New York City, calling for ICE to be abolished in the wake of a shooting by an ICE officer of Oscar Belgal, 28, while he was picking up his five-year-old child from school.
Lawyers for Belgal claimed the ICE agent did not identify himself while wearing plainclothes before he ran up to Belgal’s car, smashed in the windows, then fired several shots into the vehicle.
The Trump administration recently lost a legal challenge of New York City’s sanctuary laws filed in July 2025.

The Mamdani administration and more than 100 elected officials in New York have also urged private owners and operators of parking garages to prohibit ICE from using their private property for operations in the city.

“Our neighbors should not live in fear that the parking lot down the block could become a staging ground for an operation that puts their communities at risk,” Mamdani wrote in a 15 October letter to more than a thousand parking garage owners and operators in New York City. “I am asking every garage and lot owner in this city to stop giving them that option. Do not rent your property to ICE. Do not lend it to them. Tell them they are not welcome.”

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security told the New York Times in response to the letter: “ICE’s presence in public parking lots is fully authorized under federal law and is a standard practice for law enforcement agencies nationwide.
“Mayor Mamdani should be grateful to our brave law enforcement officers for cleaning up the streets of NYC since he won’t.”

articles.title: German Chancellor Merz wishes Koreans unity, but does Seoul really want it?
articles.summary: Germany, like Korea, was once a nation divided by rival political systems and by one of the world's most fortified borders. Chancellor Merz wished for a united Korea during his recent visit — but…

image.caption: The South Korea government officially still pursues reunification, but the younger generations' attitudes have shiftedImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The story of South and North Korea — two rival nations that share history, language and much of their cultural heritage — sounds very familiar to Germans.
Their own country spent decades divided by opposing regimes until geopolitical winds shifted and allowed East and West Germany to reunite peacefully in 1991.

Just two years later, Germany's then-Chancellor Helmut Kohl visited the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) on the Korean Peninsula and expressed hope that South and North Korea will also be reunited by the end of the decade.

His hopes never materialized. Some 35 years since Germany achieved its dream of reunification, Seoul and Pyongyang are still bitterly divided by political systems, economy, and their geopolitical alliances.
German chancellor and president tour Asia
Overlooking the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) that separates the two Korean states on Friday, current Chancellor Friedrich Merz could only rethread the wishes already stated by Kohl in 1993.

"We Germans know how painful the division of a country is," Merz stated in a message shared on social media. "We also know that whoever stands firm in their values and has the courage for dialogue can tear down walls."
"We wish the people in Korea unity in freedom," Merz added.
To analysts following the day-to-day inter-Korean politics, this sounds like a distant dream.
Young Koreans ask 'why bother' with reunification
As two Koreas continue to eye each other warily over the DMZ, their dramatic differences in wealth and political freedom are clearly on display.
But the biggest single issue might be that neither side appears to want reunification.

"The feeling has changed in the last couple of decades," said Choo Jae-woo, a professor of foreign policy at Kyung Hee University. "Younger South Koreans just see the North as another country that happens to be next to us, is poor and threatening and they have no sentimental attachment to it, like older generations do."
"More and more people are asking why they should bother about reunification," he added.
Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs

A study by Seoul National University's Institute for Peace and reunification in September indicated that 39.1% of South Koreans believed reunification was impossible, the highest proportion since the survey was started some two decades ago.
Many were concerned about the vast amounts of money it would take to build the North's infrastructure, including roads, hospitals, schools and all other requirements for a modern functioning society.

Officially, the South Korean government has not abandoned reunification as a national objective. Its constitution still calls for peaceful union based on freedom and democracy, but Choo points out recent governments are promoting the idea far less frequently than in the past.
North Korea's clear signal against unity
The North, however, has not been nearly so reticent about where it stands on the matter.

"In December 2023, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un announced that the constitution was being changed and that peaceful reunification was no longer possible," said Choo. "Instead, South Korea would be seen as a hostile rival and that he no longer had any intention of bringing the two together."
The revised North Korean constitution was approved in March 2026 and Kim's regime has moved aggressively to scrub all references to reconciliation and national unity.

"I do not think the North can make it any clearer that it has no intention of getting any closer to South Korea," said Mason Richey, a professor of politics and international relations at Hankuk University of Foreign Studies in Seoul. He added that analysts, officials and ordinary Koreans in the South "roll their eyes" when the issue of Korean reunification crops up.
Beyond the lack of desire on both sides, there are a number of additional challenges that would need to be overcome, he added.
The North Korean regime wishes to protect its own power and prestige, which would inevitably be under threat if a democratic system was introduced for a unified nation.

Bridging the enormous economic development gap would be a huge undertaking that would put immense pressure on the South, Richey said, even if outside assistance was forthcoming. And while a united Germany has been able to bring its regions to relatively comparable levels, it is worth noting that East Germany in 1990 was still substantially more developed than North Korea is today.
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
United Korea would pose major issues for US and China

Nominal GDP in North Korea is $31.7 billion a year. In the South, it is $1.85 trillion a year, or 58 times bigger, according to Bank of Korea statistics for 2024. With North Korea having roughly one-half population size of the South, the GDP per capita in the North is just $1,230 (€1,097) against nearly $36,000 in the South.

Professor Choo points out that reunification would not just be a domestic issue. The two nations have divided strategic and security loyalties, with the South allied to the US and the North tied to China and increasingly, Russia.
Why a new Russia-North Korea road bridge worries Ukraine

"Those superpowers would not want to give up their ally for reunification as it would be a major strategic issue for them as well," Choo told DW. "The US would not want a united Korea that leaned towards China and Beijing would resist reunification if it meant the US could have its military on the Chinese border in what is presently North Korea. That's just impossible for either side to imagine."

Ultimately, he said, the present status quo on the peninsula may be an imperfect solution, but it is the best way of preserving regional stability. A decade into the future, however, the economic, social and security situations may have radically altered, "and that is why we can never say never," he added.

articles.title: Colorado town braces for historic flood as heavy rains batter south-west
articles.summary:
Mandatory evacuations in Arizona and New Mexico with Pagosa Springs warned of potentially ‘catastrophic’ deluge

Heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a swath of…

blocks.text: Heavy rainfall produced flash flooding and mandatory evacuations in a swath of the south-west on Sunday, including in a Colorado tourist town bracing for its main river to rise to historic levels, as weary residents in the normally arid region deal with another drenching.

Officials in Pagosa Springs, a town of more than 2,000 in the Rockies located near ski resorts and known for its hot springs, warned of potentially “catastrophic flooding” as the San Juan River was forecast to crest at more than 20ft (6.1 meters) late on Sunday night.

“To put the forecast into perspective, during the devastating 1911 flood that wiped out most of what existed as the town of Pagosa at that time, the San Juan River crested at approximately 17.8 feet” the Archuleta county sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post. “This is a potentially catastrophic flood event.”

By sundown Sunday, the river’s crest had reached about 14 feet, according to Vicky Schaffer, a spokesperson for the county. Roads in and out of the town were closed and residents who were not under evacuation orders were urged to stay home.
Communities in northern New Mexico and central Arizona, meanwhile, also issued mandatory evacuations while the rains forced the closure of several highways.
In the picturesque town of Sedona, Arizona, officials ordered residents near Oak Creek to leave immediately as floodwaters trapped multiple people in their homes.
Arizona expects months’ worth of rain in a couple of days
Nearby Yavapai county and the community of Camp Verde issued similar evacuation orders for residents living near swollen rivers and creeks.

More than 100 miles (160km) south-east of Sedona, officials in Gila county ordered the total evacuation of Gisela, a community of several hundred residents along Tonto Creek. The wet conditions even produced flash floods, river flooding and swift boat rescues in Tucson, some 230 miles south of Sedona.
“We are getting two or three months of rain in a span of a couple of days,” said Aaron Hardin, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Tucson.

Rain fell nearly nonstop on Sunday in Flagstaff, Arizona, flooding local roads and overwhelming storm drains. Authorities were searching for a man who slipped and fell into fast-moving floodwaters “and was not seen resurfacing”, according to a police statement on Sunday evening.

The latest round of soaking rains started on Saturday evening and was expected to saturate the region through Monday. The weather service estimates as much as 4in (10cm) of rain could fall across the region, fueled by a series of Pacific storm systems.

The weather service issued flood warnings and watches for nearly all of Arizona and parts of southern Utah, south-western Colorado and western New Mexico, in addition to part of southern Nevada. That includes the sparsely populated Four Corners region where the states meet.

articles.summary:
Trump called Democratic candidate a ‘jihadist’ as El-Sayed’s defeated primary opponent backs Republican Mike Rogers. Plus an Australian fish worth its weight in gold

Good morning.…

blocks.text: Good morning. Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, has endorsed his Republican rival in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections. Tensions between El-Sayed and Stevens had already led to him asking her to stay away from his campaign events, and her endorsement of Mike Rogers comes as the US president unleashed a racist tirade against El-Sayed in Iowa.

items: What did Stevens do? Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’s endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.

What did Trump say? The president bashed El-Sayed, a practicing Muslim, in brazenly racist terms, saying that Congress would have to “get a special metal detector for Abdul” if he were elected. “If you vote for this jihadist lunatic that wants to destroy you, you’re crazy. Mike Rodgers is apple pie. And you know what this country needs? A little apple pie. We don’t need the communists or jihadists, the Muslim Brotherhood. We need apple pie.”

blocks.text: Judge dismisses Trump attempt to block Alaska Senate race results if Republican loses

blocks.caption: US senator Dan Sullivan. Photograph: Kerry Tasker/Reuters

blocks.text: A judge has dismissed the Donald Trump-backed lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate race if Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan loses. The justice department argued in its lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before election day, that there could be “voter confusion” over the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan on the November ballot. The justice department said it planned to appeal Sunday’s ruling.

According to a recent New York Times investigation, aides from Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign recruited another man who shared Sullivan’s name to join the race in a ploy to peel away votes from the Republican incumbent. Peltola has continued to deny any knowledge of such a scheme.
Investors pull billions in funds from Binance after record $6.3bn hack
Investors have pulled $3.6bn in funds from the cryptocurrency exchange Binance as it recovers from a record hack in which billions were stolen from customer accounts.

The platform was hit by a $6.3bn theft on Thursday, which has since been described as the biggest heist in history. Experts identified North Korea as the probable culprit. Binance initially froze withdrawals as it investigated the breach but on Sunday announced it had begun a phased reopening.
Israel has ‘historic’ opportunity to change direction, says leader of Arab coalition

blocks.caption: Yousef Jabareen, leader of Israel’s Arab-led Joint List political alliance. Photograph: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The leader of Israel’s main Palestinian coalition, which holds the balance of power after Tuesday’s elections, has said the country is facing a historic opportunity to change direction. Yousef Jabareen said he was ready to join forces with the Change bloc to oust Benjamin Netanyahu and his far-right coalition, and to wrest control of the Knesset.

Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, is due to summon political leaders as early as Wednesday to canvass their recommendations on who should be given the first chance to form the next government. Netanyahu’s coalition lost its majority. The Change bloc of Zionist parties led by the retired general Gadi Eisenkot has ruled out forming a unity government with Netanyahu, but also put conditions on any potential coalition with Arab parties.

Climate check: Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn

blocks.caption: A hiker dwarfed by the fracture zone of a glacier on the Greenland ice sheet. Photograph: Jason Edwards/Getty Images

blocks.text: The planet has heated by 1.3C since preindustrial times and failures to curb greenhouse gas emissions and protect nature have led scientists to conclude that some level of overshoot is inevitable as they fight to keep end-of-century warming to 1.5C. The UN report also found that Earth’s icy regions face such dangerous melting that global heating should be brought back below 1C after an inevitable period of overshooting global temperature targets.

articles.title: Global pedestrian Karl Bushby returns home to UK after 28-year trek
articles.summary: Karl Bushby, a British man who traveled 50,000 km without transport over the past 28 years, has come home. Starting in Chile, he crossed the Americas, Russia and parts of Central Asia and Europe —…

image.caption: Karl Bushby has returned home after 28 yearsImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: British adventurer Karl Bushby, 57, arrived back his hometown in England on Monday after crossing four continents on foot.
He was met by a cheering crowd of some 500 people in the northeastern city of Hull at the end of his 50,000 km (31,000 mile) journey, which began in the far south of South America in 1998.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team, Earth. That's what it took to get me back," Bushby told the crowd.
On his trip, he obeyed two rules: to avoid all forms of motorized transport to advance; and not to return until he had finished what he had set out to do.
A very final leg of his journey was to take him to north Hull, where he was to reunite with his mother, Angela, his 36-year-old son, Adam, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he had never met.

blocks.caption: Bushby was welcomed by a large crowd in his hometown of HullImage: Temilade Adelaja/REUTERS

blocks.text: What did Bushby experience on his epic journey?
Bushby, a former paratrooper, began his adventure in Chile aged 29 after a marriage breakup that saw his wife return to Northern Ireland with their son.

During the trip, he crossed an iced-over Bering Strait from Alaska to Russia with French explorer Dimitri Kieffer in 2006 — nearly losing his life in the process — and, returning to Britain early last month, he swam the English Channel from northern France to Dover over four days.

He interrupted, or was forced to pause, his journey several times, including when he was refused a visa by Russia, which caused a journey originally planned to take 12 years to last more than double that time.
He also spent some jail time in Panama for entering the country without a visa.
The COVID-19 pandemic also caused delays, and he spent some time living at a base in Mexico.
But he always resumed the trek at the exact spot where he had left off.

blocks.caption: Bushby transported the necessaries largely on a handcartImage: Paul Ellis/AFP

blocks.text: The famous German filmmaker Werner Herzog is making a feature-length documentary about the journey entitled "Walk of Life."
In an interview with the AFP news agency from northern France in September, Bushby expressed apprehension about returning to a more normal life back in Britain.
"I've got to try and get established in the grown-up world again," he said.

articles.title: ICC adopts 1-hour trial blocks with 30-minute breaks for Duterte trial
articles.summary: The ICC Trial Chamber III has adopted a trial schedule of one-hour blocks separated by 30-minute breaks for the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 8:30pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III has adopted a trial schedule of one-hour blocks separated by 30-minute breaks for the crimes against humanity case against former President Rodrigo Duterte, acting on expert advice.
Trial Chamber III adopted the modified sitting schedule during the fifth and final status conference for the case, held at the ICC in The Hague on Monday.
Duterte was not present after the court granted a defense request excusing him from the proceeding.
“In order to accommodate what the experts advised in respect to Mr. Duterte, we'll run now from 10 [a.m.] to 11 [a.m.], 11:30 [a.m.] to 12:30 [p.m.],” Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said.

“There will be a one-hour break for lunch… But I think this is necessary because of the circumstances of the case to keep those breaks and also finish at a time which allows everybody to deal with matters outside the trial,” she added.
In a decision made public on October 8, Trial Chamber III found Duterte fit to stand trial and instructed the ICC Registry to make necessary arrangements for the court proceedings.
Among the measures recommended by the Registry was a sitting schedule organized into one-hour blocks.
Under the adopted schedule, Duterte’s trial proceedings are expected to run from 10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., resume from 11:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., and break for lunch from 12:30 p.m. to 1:30 p.m.
Trial proceedings will resume from 1:30 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. and will continue following the same pattern of one-hour sessions separated by 30-minute breaks.
The trial proper in the case against Duterte is set to open on November 30, 2026. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Snowball fight: Cadbury owner in trademark row over festive chocolate treat
articles.summary: Mini Snow Balls’ maker Mondelēz is demanding vegan brand Moo Free remove its White Choccy Snowballs from shelves

blocks.text: The owner of Cadbury and Toblerone has demanded that a small vegan chocolate brand remove its products from shelves in a trademark dispute over the use of the word snowball.

Mondelēz International has written a legal letter to Moo Free accusing it of trademark infringement by selling its White Choccy Snowballs – gluten free biscuit-flavoured rice balls covered in dairy free white chocolate.

Cadbury Snowballs first launched in the UK in 1966, and have been sold in their current form as packs of Mini Snow Balls since 2023. The brand registered use of the word Snowball and Snowballs for use in chocolate confectionery as a trademark in 2001. Its Mini Snow Balls are made from Dairy Milk chocolate covered in a crispy shell of white icing sugar.

The legal fight has emerged just days after Mondelez launched legal action against another small vegan chocolate brand, Catherine’s Originals, accusing it of copying the famous chunky shape of Toblerone with its O’bar.

Moo Free, which has products stocked in several major supermarkets and online, said it had been selling its Snowballs for about two years before Mondelēz demanded it immediately remove the items from sale just ahead of the busy Christmas period.

Mike Jessop, who co-founded Devon-based Moo Free in 2010 when he and his wife could not find allergen-free chocolates for Easter or Christmas, said they began selling online before being picked up by Waitrose and then other supermarkets.

He said he had “never even heard of” Cadbury Snow Balls and was lactose intolerant so couldn’t try one. He was surprised Mondelēz had been so “heavy-handed” in its letter and questioned whether it could be possible to trademark an apparently generic term. “It’s a snowball, it is not like we are making a Freddo,” he said, referring to Cadbury’s famous frog-shaped bar.

In a letter to customers, Moo Free wrote: “Moo Free takes intellectual property concerns seriously. However, we do not accept that any infringement has been established and have responded accordingly … We are disappointed to find ourselves in this position, and we stand in solidarity with Catherine’s Originals as it addresses its own situation. We hope to resolve these matters appropriately.”

A spokesperson for Mondelēz International said: “Cadbury Snow Balls are one of our most popular Christmas products, enjoyed by households across the UK. No legal action has been taken, but we have been in touch with Moo Free to make them aware of our trademark. We are open to reaching an amicable resolution.”
It is not the UK’s first snowball fight.

Tunnock’s and Lees of Scotland won legal action against HMRC in 2014 after proving they did not have to pay VAT on their coconut-covered confections, as they were deemed sufficiently similar to a cake for an exemption. Snowballs made by these two suppliers – defined as “a dome of marshmallow coated in any combination” of chocolate, sugar strands, carob, cocoa or coconut – were subsequently given their own VAT-free status.

articles.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after two decades
articles.summary: Ugandan troops first deployed to Somalia in 2007 as part of an international military coalition to battle Islamic insurgents. But the mission has faced mounting pressure since a US decision to…

image.caption: Ugandan forces have been supporting Somali troops fighting militants for almost 20 yearsImage: Farah Abdi Warsameh/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Uganda announced on Monday that it had begun pulling its troops out of Somalia, where it has been a key player in efforts to counter insurgents for almost two decades.
"The first cohort of troops under the phased withdrawal operation have already arrived back in Uganda," a statement from the Ugandan military said.
Uganda was the first country to send troops to Somalia as part of an African Union peacekeeping force set up in 2007 to support the Somali government battling Al-Shabab Islamist militants.

Uganda "will gradually withdraw all its forces in Somalia, including those currently deployed under the African Union Support and Stabilization Mission in Somalia (AUSSOM) by the close of 2027," the military's statement added, referring to the latest African Union mission.
Around 4,500 Ugandan troops are stationed in Somalia as part of AUSSOM, as well as about 2,000 deployed under bilateral agreements.

The Ugandan army said its withdrawal "will mark the end of Uganda's enduring 20-year peace and stabilization support operations in Somalia, permitting the Somali Armed Forces to assume full responsibility for security in the country."
Jihadist groups in Africa and their links
An initial contingent of 109 Ugandan soldiers left the Somali capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, local media reported.
Why is Uganda withdrawing its troops from Somalia?
The future of the African Union mission, AUSSOM, has been thrown into doubt following a recent US decision to end funding for a UN logistics office the military coalition relies on.

Washington, the coalition's biggest donor, has voiced frustration with a lack of progress in the fight against Al-Shabab, which continues to control large swaths of central Somalia. The US has also accused the Somali government of failing to unite the country and implement political reforms.
Somali civilians caught in crossfire as US strikes militants
Uganda's withdrawal announcement on Monday also came as the UN ended its political mission in Somalia.

The UN Transitional Assistance Mission in Somalia closed on Saturday after more than three decades of peacebuilding in the East African country, transferring responsibility to the Somali government and various UN agencies.
Somalia is due to hold elections in May next year, but insecurity and opposition disputes are threatening to derail the process.

Somalia has been gripped by a deadly insurgency led by Al-Shabab for more than two decades. While Ugandan forces have played a crucial role in driving the militants from the capital and several major towns, the group has recaptured territory in recent years and now controls significant areas in the center and south of the country.

articles.title: Duterte trial: ICC rejects victims' request to use Tagalog in opening statement
articles.summary: Judges at the International Criminal Court have refused a request to use Tagalog during opening statements in the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

blocks.text: November 2, 2026 | 8:16pm
Families of extrajudicial killing victims attend a Catholic Mass at the House of Representatives prior to the eighth hearing on EJKs on Oct. 11, 2024.
House of Representatives / Release
MANILA, Philippines — Judges at the International Criminal Court have refused a request to use Tagalog during opening statements in the trial of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

During the final status conference on Monday, November 2, lawyers for the victims had asked if they could deliver their remarks in Tagalog for about 15 to 20 minutes to be better understood by other victims who will be following the proceedings in the Philippines.

"For them, it's also important to listen to how we convey to the Chamber what they narrated to us and their experiences, and they relate and connect much more if that is done in Tagalog," Paolina Massidda, principal counsel of the Office of Public Counsel for Victims, said.

Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said the Rome Statute, the court’s founding treaty, sets English and French as the court’s working languages. Using any other language would require a "really exceptional reason," he said.
Such requests are becoming “a recurring theme” across ICC trials, Korner commented.
"One of the problems is that the moment we start to do this, then applications come in and it becomes much more complicated and more expensive if we accede to it," Korner said.
Korner also noted that not all the victims speak Tagalog and that the proceedings would be interpreted.
She said she would ask the court’s registry whether a Tagalog translation or transcript could be published on the ICC website.
Duterte did not attend Monday’s hearing, the last status conference before his trial opens November 30.
Korner said he had been excused “exceptionally” because the session was not expected to be long.
Once the trial begins, Duterte will be expected to attend every day.
The chamber also shortened its sitting day for the first weeks of the trial.
Hearings will run from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Hague time, with a break after every hour, to accommodate medical experts’ advice regarding Duterte.

articles.title: Iliana Yotova wins the presidential election in Bulgaria, portraying herself as the 'president of peace'
articles.summary: Iliana Yotova won the presidential election in Bulgaria, promising to be a "president of peace." But the campaign showed how divided Bulgarians are about the war in Ukraine and drone attacks in the…

image.caption: Iliana Yotova (center) won the Bulgarian presidential election runoff decisively on Sunday, garnering 57.6% of the vote. She is pictured addressing the press after the first exit polls gave her a clear leadImage: BGNES

blocks.text: "We are choosing between war and peace," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told voters ahead of Sunday's presidential election runoff between incumbent President Iliana Yotova, who opposes military aid to Ukraine and favors dialogue with Russia, and former caretaker Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov, who is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-Ukrainian.
With these words, it was clear that Sunday's runoff had turned into a kind of referendum on the country's foreign policy and stance on the war in Ukraine.
Now that the official results are in and it is clear that Iliana Yotova won the election decisively by 57.6% to Gyurov's 39.5%, Radev claims that Bulgarians have chosen peace.
But is it really as simple as all that?
First-round surprise

When the presidential election campaign began in Bulgaria on September 25, there did not seem to be any doubt about the outcome: Iliana Yotova was well ahead in the polls on 44.5%. Gyurov, her main rival, trailed far behind on 26.1%.
Yotova was backed by both the prime minister and his ruling Progressive Bulgaria party, which won an absolute majority in the parliamentary election on April 19.

blocks.caption: Yotova, who succeeded Ruman Radev as president when he stepped down to run for prime minister earlier this year, is the first woman to be elected president of BulgariaImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: But the first round turned out to be much tighter than anticipated.
While Yotova got 34.8% of the vote in the first round, Gyurov was close behind on 31.95%, which meant that a runoff between the two was necessary.
Decisive victory, clear divide
While Yotova won the runoff convincingly, both the campaign and the outcome showed that the Bulgarian electorate is divided.
This division is both generational and geographical, explains Dimitar Ganev, sociologist and political scientist at the Trend market and electoral research agency.

"Younger voters — those aged between 18 and 40 — favor Gyurov. Those over 40 tend to prefer Yotova," Ganev told DW. "It also appears that Gyurov dominates in the capital, Sofia. In smaller regional cities, other towns and villages, Yotova dominates decisively," he said.
'President of peace'
This divide was also evident during the campaign.

blocks.caption: Candidates Andrey Gyurov (left) and Iliana Yotova (right) faced each other in Sunday's presidential election runoffImage: Desislava Kulelieva/BNT

blocks.text: While Andrey Gyurov relied mainly on social media for his campaign, Yotova chose to speak mostly to supporters of Progressive Bulgaria in closed venues.
At such events, the war in Ukraine was always high on the agenda.

"As long as I am president, and if you place your trust in me, not a single Bulgarian soldier will go to Ukraine," Yotova declared at an election rally on October 6 — even though according to the Bulgarian Constitution, only parliament (not the president) has the authority to send troops abroad or declare war.
Throughout the campaign, she referred to her opponents as "warmongers" and described herself as the "president of peace."
"We won because we talked to people about income and about peace," Yotova said after the election.
Russia's war in Ukraine a major campaign issue
In this, she is similar to Prime Minister Rumen Radev.

When it comes to Ukraine, Radev regularly speaks of the need for peace and avoids calling Russia an "aggressor." Both Radev and Yotova oppose military aid to Ukraine and criticize European leaders for not making sufficient efforts to engage with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Gyurov, on the other hand, has sharply criticized Russian aggression in Ukraine.
Appointed caretaker prime minister by Yotova in February, Gyurov in March signed a security cooperation agreement with Ukraine, provoking the disapproval of both Yotova and Radev.
The impact of drone attacks in the Black Sea
In the weeks leading up to the election, several ships in the Black Sea were hit by drones off the Bulgarian coast.

blocks.caption: Bulgaria's former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov is regarded as staunchly pro-European and pro-UkrainianImage: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP

blocks.text: The European Council criticized Russia for the escalation, and the European Parliament called on the EU and its member states "to consider deploying an EU naval operation" there.

Prime Minister Radev, however, was not as equivocal, going no further than summoning the Russian ambassador and stating that "logic suggests that the outcome" of the attacks in the Black Sea "is to the advantage of the Russian Federation."
Just days before the runoff, he noted that "two ships were struck and sunk in Romanian territorial waters" after Romania had held Russia responsible for the attacks in the Black Sea.

"Many people think that once the aggressor is identified, the attacks will stop," he said, downplaying the Kremlin's responsibility. His remarks drew criticism from politicians and the media in Romania.

Yotova also did not name Russia as the perpetrator, instead saying during her campaign that she did not want to see "foreign flags in Bulgaria" — a clear reference to the Ukrainian flag, which has been displayed outside several institutions in Bulgaria as a sign of solidarity with the war-torn country.
How other voters voted

Most opposition parties, including the right-wing conservative GERB led by former long-serving Prime Minister Boyko Borisov, refused to field a candidate for the presidency, which is one reason why turnout on Sunday was less than 30%.

In the first round, the pro-Russian candidate Kostadin Kostadinov from the nationalist Vazrazhdane (Revival) party came third with 12.5% of the vote. According to Dimitar Ganev, around 70% of Vazrazhdane voters backed Yotova in the runoff.
To secure their support, Yotova targeted pro-Russian voters.
How Russian aggression is shaping Bulgaria's presidential election

"Russia is by no means an enemy of Bulgaria," she said in a podcast interview just two days before the runoff, adding "Russia is part of our history, and I very much hope that it will be a key factor in the future security architecture across Europe, including for us."

In the days leading up to the vote, some of her supporters began claiming that the opposition was preparing a "Maidan," a reference to the Ukrainian revolution of 2014 that culminated in the ousting of President Viktor Yanukkovych, who had close ties to Moscow.

"All of Gyurov's lackeys are speaking openly about inevitable protests. They're using prime time to stir up a Maidan. Every single one of them," Sonya Momchilova, who was appointed to the media regulator by Radev, wrote on Facebook on Sunday.
Similar claims were made by both former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban and former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic ahead of this year's elections in their countries.
Bulgaria in the EU and NATO

"This claim that Ms. Yotova will be a president of peace is directly linked to the incitement of a fear of war," said former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, who was part of the committee that nominated Andrey Gyurov for president. "Bulgaria will be in a much worse position within Europe and NATO under her leadership," he said during a TV interview.

Dimitar Ganev, on the other hand, sees no threat to Bulgaria's commitment to the EU and NATO. "Over two-thirds of Bulgarians do not question the country's geopolitical orientation, and around two-thirds have a positive attitude towards the EU," he told DW.

But the positions of Radev and Yotova, which many view as ambivalent, mobilized both the pro-European camp and Eurosceptic voters, who, according to Ganev, make up around a third of the country's population.
According to Prime Minister Rumen Radev and President Iliana Yotova, the Bulgarian people chose peace in the presidential election. Nevertheless, the war continues.

articles.title: Magic: The Gathering's Star Trek Commander Decks
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Final Frontier is making its way to the Commander table as Star Trek joins Magic: The Gathering (MTG) with four new preconstructed decks set to release on November 13, 2026.…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The Final Frontier is making its way to the Commander table as Star Trek joins Magic: The Gathering (MTG) with four new preconstructed decks set to release on November 13, 2026.
As the final major release in MTG’s 2026 lineup, the Star Trek collaboration brings some of the franchise’s most recognizable characters, factions, and locations to the trading card game.
From the Federation and its diverse roster of species to the war-driven Klingons and the ever-expanding Borg Collective, there’s plenty for Trekkies and MTG players to discover.
Featuring four ready-to-play 100-card Commander decks, the collection offers different playstyles inspired by the Star Trek universe.
Whether you’re looking to explore strange new worlds, lead the Federation, wage Klingon warfare, or assimilate your opponents, here’s what to expect from each deck.
RELATED STORY: Magic: The Gathering Foundations Commander decks explained
Federation Fleet
Federation Fleet is a Blue-Red-White Commander deck led by Jean-Luc Picard, Luminary.
Built around drawing cards and playing historic spells and permanents, the deck rewards players for maintaining a steady flow of cards throughout the game.

It’s a particularly appealing choice for fans of Star Trek: The Next Generation (TNG).Its primary mechanic, Seek Out, triggers whenever you draw your second card each turn, including during your opponents’ turns.
This makes card draw an important part of the deck’s strategy, allowing players to generate additional value while keeping their options open.
Players can also switch things up by replacing Picard with the deck’s alternate commander, Captain Janeway, Endgame.
Rather than focusing on historic cards, Janeway rewards players for dealing combat damage with Officers.

Whenever an Officer deals damage, she lets you draw a card and create another Officer token, giving the deck an alternative way to trigger Seek Out while building a stronger board presence.Other cards, such as Ro Laren, Double Agent and Rom and Leeta, Unlikely Pair, further support the deck’s strategy by providing additional engines and payoffs for its card-drawing synergies.
Landing Party
Landing Party is a Green-White-Blue Commander deck helmed by Commander Spock, with an emphasis on its Strange New Worlds mechanic.
This ability rewards players for having lands with different names on the battlefield, complementing the deck’s secondary Landfall strategy, which triggers whenever a land enters the battlefield.
With the goal of building a diverse collection of lands as quickly as possible, Landing Party encourages players to explore different ways of developing their mana base.
The more unique lands you have in play, the more you can take advantage of the deck’s Strange New Worlds synergies.
For players who would rather take a different approach, the deck also features Captain Kirk, Boldly Going as an alternate commander.
While Landfall remains an important part of the strategy, Kirk shifts the focus toward the Starship Enterprise and its supporting crew.
Cards like Chief Kyle, Transporter Tech and Lt. Arex, Ever-Adapting generate additional value as lands enter the battlefield.
Meanwhile, reprints such as Exploration and Ancient Greenwarden help maximize Landfall triggers, allowing players to get even more mileage out of every land drop.
Klingon Fury
Klingon Fury is a Red-White-Black Commander deck led by Worf, Defiant Commander.
True to its color identity and aggressive playstyle, the deck focuses on dealing damage to opponents through its primary mechanic, Battlefront.
Battlefront abilities reward players for attacking multiple opponents in a single turn, making the deck particularly effective in multiplayer Commander games.
Worf takes advantage of this mechanic by generating additional value whenever its conditions are met, encouraging players to keep the pressure on and spread their attacks across the table.
Alternatively, players can put Kor, Cause of Vengeance at the helm of their Klingon-themed army.
Rather than relying on Worf’s value-generation strategy, Kor focuses on strengthening Klingon and Warrior creatures.
His ability provides +2/+2 boosts and card draw when another creature is sacrificed, giving players another way to maintain their offensive momentum.

The rest of the deck supports this aggressive strategy with cards like The Sword of Kahless, which provides additional board presence during attacks, and I.K.S. Negh’Var, Imperial Flagship, which grants Vigilance to Klingon and Warrior creatures.
Klingon Fury also features a potentially devastating infinite combat interaction involving the reprinted card Combat Celebrant.
Additional cards like Professional Face-Breaker help maintain the deck’s momentum, making it an appealing option for players who prefer an aggressive approach to Commander.
We Are the Borg
We Are the Borg is a White-Blue-Black Commander deck led by The Borg Queen, the personification of the Borg Collective’s hivemind.
While it might initially appear to be another artifact-focused deck, its real strategy revolves around assimilation.

Inspired by the Borg’s ability to absorb other species into its collective, the deck’s Assimilate mechanic transforms opposing creatures into Borg artifacts, allowing players to expand their own forces using their opponents’ resources.

The Borg Queen’s seven-mana cost makes her a relatively expensive commander to cast, but her ability to assimilate creatures whenever she enters the battlefield or attacks makes her a formidable presence once she’s in play.
Players can also opt for Locutus of Borg as their alternate commander, offering another way to build and expand a Borg army.

The rest of the deck supports this strategy by strengthening artifact creatures and artifact spells, with cards like Hugh, First of Many providing Replicate and One, Borg Evolved serving as a potential finisher.
Reprints such as Tempered Steel and Forsaken Monument further strengthen the deck’s artifact-based strategy.
If taking control of the battlefield and turning your opponents’ forces against them sounds appealing, We Are the Borg might be the Commander deck for you.
Exploring a New Frontier
With the holiday season approaching, Star Trek’s Commander decks could make for an interesting Christmas gift for fans of both Magic: The Gathering and the iconic science fiction franchise.
Each deck offers a distinct playstyle, giving newcomers an opportunity to explore Commander while offering longtime players new cards and strategies to add to their collections.
Beyond their gameplay mechanics, the decks also feature artwork inspired by the Star Trek universe, complete with references to memorable characters and moments from the franchise.
These details make the collection particularly appealing to Trekkies who want to see their favorite parts of the series brought to the Commander table.

Whether you want to boldly explore strange new worlds, lead the Federation, unleash Klingon fury, or assimilate everything in your path, Star Trek’s arrival in MTG offers plenty of ways to experience the Final Frontier.

The Star Trek Commander decks will be available in both regular and Collector’s Edition versions, with the latter featuring Surge Foil treatments across the entire deck. Both editions are scheduled for release on November 13, 2026.

articles.title: Canadian among the dead in Spanish high-speed rail crash
articles.summary: A Canadian was among those killed last week in a high-speed train collision in Toledo, Spanish officials have said, issuing a list of countries whose citizens died in the Oct. 28 tragedy.

image.caption: People are shown at a funeral mass on Saturday for the 69 fatal victims of a high-speed train collision last week in Toledo, Spain. (Thomas Coex/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New
A Canadian was among those killed last week in a high-speed train collision in Toledo, Spanish officials have said, issuing a list of countries whose citizens died in the Oct. 28 tragedy.
Citizens from several countries died in crash, along with 54 Spaniards
A Canadian was among those killed last week in a high-speed train collision in Toledo, Spanish officials have said.

The Tribunal Superior de Justicia de Castilla La Mancha issued a statement Sunday, providing more information about the 69 people who died, after the victims were identified by the country's Center for Integrated Data.

Global Affairs Canada (GAC) told CBC News last week that it was aware of six Canadians who were injured in the crash and one person who was unaccounted for. The department, citing privacy considerations, provided no further information. The department did not immediately respond to an updated request for information.
Also among the dead were 54 people from Spain, along with citizens from France, the United States, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia, Portugal and the Czech Republic, Spanish officials have said.
The crash, affecting 526 passengers and 12 crew members overall on the two trains, happened near the town of Urda in central Spain on Oct. 28.

It was the second major fatal accident this year involving the same rail companies on the same line after a January crash killed 46, reopening a debate about safety and maintenance on Spain's high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe.
Did human error cause Spain's deadly high-speed train crash? | About That

The collision occurred after several trains were automatically stopped due to the failure of the automatic-signalling system, after which the central control centre in Madrid took over. A train operated by state-owned Renfe was authorized to proceed, even though there was a stationary Iryo-operated train ahead, according to Transport Minister Óscar Puente.
Puente has thus far resisted calls from opposition parties to resign.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez visited the crash site late last week and has pledged an investigation into the latest collision and improvements to prevent another tragedy.
The crash occurs as Sánchez and his Socialists are campaigning to stay in power, ahead of a Nov. 29 election.

The Spanish government was already facing discontent over housing costs and high rents, along with corruption allegations and criticism from right-wing parties of its liberal migration policies compared to other European countries.
With files from The Associated Press and Reuters

articles.title: UK’s largest brickmaker hit by sales slump as housebuilding downturn deepens
articles.summary:
Ibstock, which has cut production by a fifth, criticises government for delay in help for housing sector

Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as…

blocks.text: Sales at the UK’s largest brickmaker plunged by more than a fifth over the summer, as it criticised the government for not introducing fresh help for the housing sector faster.
Leicestershire-based Ibstock said on Monday that sales slumped by 22% below its expectations in the quarter to the end of September, prompting it to slash production levels by a fifth.

Ibstock issued its second profit warning this year and said that UK brick market volumes declined by 17% year on year in July and August, with weak market conditions continuing through September and October.

“Trading conditions deteriorated sharply during the third quarter, with weakness continuing into October,” said Joe Hudson, the chief executive of Ibstock. “We have responded by reducing production to manage inventory, taking further cost action and maintaining tight control of cash. These production decisions create an additional near-term earnings headwind but are necessary to align output with demand.”

The warning by the company, which now expects full-year profits to be “materially below” previous expectations, comes days after the Office for Budget Responsibility cut its forecast for the number of new homes that will be built by 2031 by 190,000.

Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, has admitted there is only a “slim chance” the government will meet its goal of building 1.5m new homes this parliament, amid estimates it could miss the target by a third.

Shares in Ibstock plunged more than 8% as the company also criticised the government’s decision not to start the Your First Home support scheme, which is designed to help first-time buyers in England buy a new-build home with a 2.5% deposit, until next April.

“The introduction of the Your First Home support scheme represents a welcome and potentially meaningful intervention for the UK housing market, with the potential to improve affordability, stimulate new-build demand and strengthen confidence in future housing supply,” the company said. “While the announcement reinforces confidence in the group’s medium-term market outlook, the delay to its introduction until April 2027 is disappointing and has put additional pressure on near-term demand.”
Ibstock said it now expects full-year profits to be in the mid-£40m range, well down on analysts’ previous consensus of £59m.
after newsletter promotion
The company said its cost savings and cash management initiatives are focused primarily on overhead and discretionary spend.

“Domestically exposed building stocks like Ibstock continue to face very challenging industry conditions,” said Clyde Lewis and Sam Cullen, analysts at Peel Hunt, in a note to investors. “The new Your First Home programme should be modestly helpful next year but lower interest rates remain key to a pickup in sector activity and share prices.”
