articles.title: Ryanair considers pay freezes and reducing crew on flights as fuel costs soar
articles.summary:
Airline also weighs up increasing use of AI as part of cost-cutting measures to offset impact of Iran war

Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including implementing pay freezes,…

blocks.text: Ryanair is considering cost-cutting measures including implementing pay freezes, reducing crew on flights and increasing the use of AI to offset soaring fuel costs because of the Middle East conflict.

Europe’s biggest low-cost carrier said it expects European airlines to raise their ticket prices by as much as 20%, as it anticipates its jet fuel costs will increase by about €2bn (£1.6bn) in its next financial year, which ends in March 2028.

“Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict we expect jet fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027,” said Michael O’Leary, the chief executive of Ryanair. “While we believe European short-haul fares will increase materially to reflect these much higher jet-fuel prices and competitor capacity reductions, this is unlikely to provide a full offset for an estimated €2bn increase in our fuel bill.”
The oil price hit a six-month high last Friday but fell on Monday to about $110 a barrel.
Ryanair said it expects European short-haul fares will “increase materially” next year as a result, as the oil hedging deals taken out by airlines to reduce costs come to an end.

“To help address this, we’re reviewing all costs across group airlines with a particular focus on airport churn negotiations, maturing labour agreements (which may require temporary pay freezes), lower crew ratios and increased use of AI,” O’Leary said.
The company said the AI drive would be focused on “further operational and back office/support functions” productivity.
Ryanair said its fuel requirements through to the end of March remain 80% hedged at $67 a barrel.
The company’s hedges for the following 12 months are 25% hedged at $95 a barrel.

The Irish airline, Europe’s largest in terms of passenger numbers, said that average fares fell by 2% year on year in the quarter to the end of September. Ryanair added that fare prices in the final three months of the year were trending “modestly ahead” of the same quarter last year.
after newsletter promotion

“The booking window remains closer-in which reduces visibility,” the company said.“[The current quarter’s] fare outcome will heavily depend on the strength of close-in October-November school midterm [holiday] and Christmas bookings.”

The airline reported a post-tax profit of €1.61bn in the quarter to the end of September, a fall of 6% year on year but in line with analyst expectations. Passenger numbers grew 5% year on year to 64.5 million for the quarter.

articles.title: Who’s coddling Bato dela Rosa? Not us, says MNLF
articles.summary: The Moro National Liberation Front quickly distances itself from the fugitive senator, after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Dela Rosa is being protected by an 'armed group' in Mindanao

blocks.text: BATO. Senator Ronald 'Bato' dela Rosa attends the Senate plenary session on May 12, 2026.
The Moro National Liberation Front quickly distances itself from the fugitive senator, after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said Dela Rosa is being protected by an 'armed group' in Mindanao
If Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is, indeed, hiding in Mindanao, the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) insists they’re not the ones sheltering him.

In a statement, the MNLF denied it is the “powerful armed group” that had been “cuddling” (or shouldn’t that be coddling?) Dela Rosa, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) over his alleged role in the bloody drug war of the Rodrigo Duterte administration.
“The MNLF is not cuddling Senator Bato. There is no established formal relationship between Sen. Ronald ‘Bato’ dela Rosa and the MNLF,” the group said in its statement.
Dela Rosa has been out of public view since May amid the ICC arrest warrant.
The MNLF made the statement after Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla said that he had received information that the legislator was being protected by an “armed” group in Mindanao.
Remulla had also warned that attempting a forced arrest on the lawmaker could cost “10,000” lives, to explain why he would rather negotiate the senator’s surrender.

The interior chief did not identify the alleged armed group. The MNLF, however, was quick to distance itself from the speculation, saying the personal ties between former president Rodrigo Duterte and MNLF founder Nur Misuari should not be construed as evidence that the group was hiding dela Rosa.

“The claim that the MNLF may be protecting him is speculation, not a confirmed fact. Reports emphasize that the MNLF is fragmented and that it is uncertain whether the Misuari faction would-or could-shield him from arrest,” the group said.

“So, the accurate answer is: dela Rosa appears to have personal and political connections to figures associated with the MNLF, especially through Duterte’s relationship with Nur Misuari, but there is no verified evidence that he is an MNLF member, ally in an operational sense, or currently being protected by the group,” it added.

Partido Demokratiko Pilipino Lakas ng Bayan, Dela Rosa’s political party, has appealed to the Supreme Court for a swift resolution of Dela Rosa’s case. The senator’s camp also urged the High Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an ICC warrant of arrest against him.
But with the senator still nowhere to be found, could his arrest be drawing closer?
The Philippine National Police has intensified its manhunt for its former chief after the one-week deadline for his voluntary surrender lapsed.
Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson, who previously called for Dela Rosa’s safe arrest, has a reminder for authorities: Keep their operations under wraps.

“When pursuing a high-profile target or handling a sensitive live case, secrecy discipline is key — unless disinformation is necessary to flush the quarry into the open,” Lacson, a former PNP chief, said in a social media post.
Did Lacson have anyone in particular in mind when he gave the unsolicited advice? – Rappler.com

articles.title: Canada had more than 220 gambler suicides in last decade — but no inquests
articles.byline: Dave Seglins, Saloni Bhugra, Andreas Wesley

image.caption: As gambling expands in Canada, experts call on coroners to do a better job of investigating and tracking gambling related deaths. (Julien de Rosa/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: This story is part of a CBC News series examining the public health impacts of online gambling.
Dave, a retiree recovering from gambling addiction, says that when he was winning, he felt like a king, hooked by the prospect of wealth and recognition.
But he says like most gamblers, he "inevitably" started losing.

"Not only money — trust, people we care for, spouses, children, we lose the whole gamut. Everything that we built goes crumbling down," he told CBC News during a recent online Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto.
"So we often try suicide, which I did try. I turned out to be an utter failure at that."
CBC reporter Dave Seglins speaks to a Gamblers Anonymous meeting in Toronto. (Ousama Abdel Rahman/CBC)
A CBC News investigation has found that at least 220 problem gamblers in Canada have died by suicide in the last decade, which includes a tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022.

items: Ontario sees surge in gambling addiction, suicides after expansion

blocks.text: But the national numbers are likely higher, as Alberta, Saskatchewan, Nova Scotia, Yukon and Nunavut don’t track gambling-related deaths, citing a lack of obvious indicators in most death investigations.

What’s more, no coroner in Canada has ever held an inquest into the issue — unlike in Australia and the United Kingdom, where inquests are being used to critically examine the gambling industry and the links between addiction and suicide.
'Misery and great harm'
A coroner in Australia delivered a scathing inquest report last month, calling for major industry reforms after investigating the suicide of 22-year-old Kyle Hudson.
Hudson opened online betting accounts after his 18th birthday and over four years, placed more than 10,000 bets, losing a cumulative $47,000 Cdn.
The morning he died, he had placed and lost bets worth $6,200.
Coroner Paul Lowrie concluded that Hudson’s preferred platform, SportsBet, ought to have detected his problem gambling.

"Kyle’s case reveals, in the sharpest relief, the human cost of online gambling," the coroner wrote. "It should be a clear signal that we cannot leave monitoring and intervention solely in the hands of the betting companies."
Kyle Hudson was 'a young man brimming with promise,' according to a coroner's report in Australia. He was working part-time while in his fourth year at university and loved sport. (ABC.net.au)
Hudson’s betting escalated and triggered 37 alerts on SportBet’s internal "Safer Gambling" monitoring system, the inquest heard.
The company sent him automated support emails and on multiple occasions called him to suspend his account, only to receive a call back from Hudson, who convinced them to reinstate it.
SportsBet also sent Hudson hundreds of bonus offers and inducements to continue playing, which the coroner found to be "contrary" to the company’s safer gambling programs.
"These products are carefully designed to keep gamblers engaged and active, and to extract net losses over time," Lowrie wrote.
"They are dangerous and capable of causing misery and great harm, especially for the young or those whose traits may make them more vulnerable."
SportsBet maintained during the inquest that Hudson did not have a gambling problem. That’s despite accounts from Hudson’s family, experts and analysis of the extent of his online gambling activity.
"It is chilling that this is SportsBet’s view," Lowrie concluded.
LISTEN | The Big Bet:
Understood: The Big Bet2:32Introducing The Big Bet
Inquests examine gambling companies' player data
Charles Ritchie of Sheffield, England, who started the charity Gambling With Lives, says inquests are an important tool to change laws and cast light on the gambling industry.
He became an advocate after his 24-year-old son Jack took his own life in November 2017.

"We realized straight away that it was gambling that had killed him. It was there in his suicide note," Ritchie told CBC News, detailing how Jack had started gambling as a teen and got hooked online after a fluke win of 1,000 pounds ($1,870 Cdn) on an electronic gaming terminal.
Jack Ritchie’s online gambling addiction led to his death, a U.K. coroner found. (Leigh Day law firm)
Ritchie says an inquest into Jack’s death in 2022 validated that it was caused by gambling.
Beyond that, he says inquests have become a valuable tool for grieving families to hold companies accountable if they have failed to intervene in cases of addiction.
Gambling apps can spot warning signs, says watchdog
After someone’s death, he says inquests can analyze the deceased’s behaviour using player data and banking records.

"When we look at those figures in the raw… Somebody is, at four o'clock in the morning, having hundreds of bets, is losing hundreds of pounds. You as a human being would say, ‘This is wrong. We need to intervene,’" he said.
"Gambling companies don't do that. And that has been found in so many of the inquests."
The U.K. has held inquests into the gambling deaths of, clockwise from top left, Arthur Soames, Jack Ritchie, Oliver Long, Gareth Evans, Luke Ashton, Ellen Mulvey and Lee Adams. (Leigh Day law firm)
No inquests in Canada
The U.K. has held seven gambling-related inquests since Jack Ritchie’s death inquiry in 2022, resulting in numerous recommendations to the government and the gambling industry.
Coroners and medical examiners in Canada have never undertaken a similar investigation.
CBC contacted chief coroners and medical examiners across Canada, who acknowledge not every jurisdiction tracks gambling suicides.
Nor do most coroners consider whether problem gambling was a contributing factor during suicide investigations. It can be hard to detect without an explicit suicide note.

People with gambling addictions tend to hide their problem from family and friends. Coroners don’t routinely probe a suicide victim’s financial records or online history to determine whether they had a gambling problem.
Journalist Rob Csernyik, author of A Losing Hand: The Human Cost of Canada’s Gambling Epidemic, says chief coroners pledged in 2003 to begin tracking the problem nationally. It has never happened.
"It's just something that hasn't been on the radar in many years in Canada, despite the expansion of gambling," Csernyik told CBC News.
Canada lacks data on gambling suicides, despite the expansion of online betting, says author and journalist Rob Csernyik. (Roger Cosman/CBC)
"I think that now with the larger push into legal gambling markets, that it's something we finally need to address."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022, the year the province legalized private online betting, worries him that we'll see an epidemic of addiction.
"This is the thing I’ve been fearful for," said Kelly, an adolescent addiction specialist in Ottawa.
He’s calling for much closer monitoring of problem gambling as well as restrictions on gambling advertising to curb gambling’s harms before they get worse.
"To me, it would be much too late to act when we had irrefutable evidence that our changes in gambling legislation have led to an increase in suicide amongst the vulnerable."
Dr. Shawn Kelly says the tripling of gambling-related suicides in Ontario since 2022 is a warning sign for public health officials. (Ousama Farag/CBC)
CBC asked Ontario’s Ministry of Health to comment on the rise in gambling addiction and related suicides in the province.
The minister’s press secretary deferred to Ontario’s Ministry of Tourism, Culture and Gaming, which oversees the province’s $3-billion-a-year online gambling market.

The Gaming Ministry did not address the rise in suicide rates but said in an email that since 2018, "our government has invested $421 million, including $70.1 million over the last year, in responsible gambling education, research and addiction treatment."
In the meantime, members at Gamblers Anonymous, a peer-to-peer support group with chapters around the world, are hoping more people who are struggling reach out for help.
Dan, who like Dave considered suicide, describes the group as a "big extended family."

"If I didn't find GA (Gamblers Anonymous), there's a very solid chance that either I'd be living on the streets, lost my home, marriage or even dead," he told CBC News. "That came across my mind many times."
Gamblers Anonymous 'saved my life,' says recovering gambler
Are you, or someone you know, suffering from gambling? Support is available.

Gamblers Anonymous 1-855-222-5542 or visit Canada or Toronto/GTA

articles.title: Hudson Williams talks tattoos, sex scenes, Connor Storrie with neurodivergent interviewers in The Assembly S2
articles.summary: Hudson Williams answered a range of questions from autistic and neurodivergent interviewers in Season 2 of The Assembly. Here are five things we learned about the Heated Rivalry star.

image.caption: Hudson Williams opens up to a roomful of autistic and neurodivergent interviewers in Season 2 of The Assembly on CBC. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New
Hudson Williams answered a range of questions from autistic and neurodivergent interviewers in Season 2 of The Assembly. Here are five things we learned about the Heated Rivalry star.
5 things we learned from the Heated Rivalry star's revealing interview
Hudson Williams — whose own father is on the autism spectrum — rose to fame playing Shane Hollander, a world-class hockey player who is also on the spectrum, in Heated Rivalry.
So what did he say when he was invited to be questioned by a roomful of autistic and neurodivergent interviewers?
"I'm strapped in. My knees are bent."
The rules of The Assembly are as follows: "No subjects are out of bounds. No questions are off the table, and all might happen."
The first episode of Season 2 aired on CBC television last night and can still be viewed on Gem. To avoid spoilers, stream it now before reading any further.
The meaning behind one of his tattoos

Hudson Williams gives a bit of a tattoo tour at the start of his episode on The Assembly. As the room fills up, he shows the interviewers which ones were done by his tattoo-artist girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.
The cherries just above his left elbow, for starters. And higher up on his shoulder, the outline of a set of teeth.
It's the underbite of his late dog, Jesse Skywalker Williams, who died at 17 years old, he says.
"Whenever he looked at me, he had this little underbite smile," says Williams.

items: Hudson Williams's girlfriend says Heated Rivalry fans crossing 'huge boundary'

blocks.text: How Hudson Williams views his relationship with Connor Storrie

True to The Assembly's promise, one interviewer named Nate asks Williams what many people have been wondering but may have been too afraid to ask: "Did you ever feel something for Connor that was more than friendship?"
Williams says he and his Heated Rivalry co-star Connor Storrie are "platonic soulmates — just completely in love with each other."
But he makes it clear those feelings will never become romantic — not even if they cuddle for 10 hours straight. He says it's what makes their relationship stable and beautiful.
Though Williams does suggest it would be great to bring Storrie everywhere — even the shower.
"Someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day…. Because I have a loofah, but I can't reach. If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there."
In Season 2 of The Assembly, Williams answers questions about his Heated Rivalry co-stars and what it’s really like filming those steamy sex scenes. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)
When the interview ends, that revelation inspires another member of The Assembly to share that he has a guy he loves too: his best friend Colin.
"That's lovely. It's so important to have that," Williams tells him.
He was 'pumped' for friends and family to watch Heated Rivalry sex scenes
Williams says he wasn't worried about those closest to him seeing the intimate scenes in Heated Rivalry.
In fact, he held a screening for the first episode and invited about a dozen friends plus his mom to watch it together, with the expectation it would be "the best friends-screening ever."
Any time a sex scene was coming up, Williams would tell his mom to cover her eyes. His friends all brought party horns, which they blew any time something provocative was happening on screen.
When the horns went silent, his mom knew it was safe to start watching again.
His controversial Victoria comment was taken out of context
When Williams was filming Yaga back in March, he described Victoria in a way that stirred up controversy online.
Specifically, he described it as "dead as f**k" and full of "old people."

The autistic and neurodivergent interviewers in The Assembly asked Williams a range of questions, including what his workouts were like and whether he ever caught feelings for his co-star Connor Storrie. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)
An interviewer named Margot gives Williams the opportunity to set the record straight, and he takes it, telling her the quote was taken out of context.

"I was like, 'Oh my God, I'm doing so much better. I'm filming this show and I just love it. It's so great. I'm shooting in Victoria, which is like dead as f**k, old people, boring.' Like, I was using those adjectives to describe why I love it."
Williams says he never meant "old people" to be taken as an insult, but he's learning this is all part of being in the public eye.

items: Yaga TV show packed with lore and Canadian talent — including Hudson Williams

blocks.text: Williams says he ignored ADHD symptoms
One of the questions Williams appears to appreciate most comes from an interviewer named Julia: "How do you feel like your Korean values have shaped your experience of having ADHD?"
Williams describes how for a long time he struggled to focus in class, and he says his background may have contributed to him ignoring symptoms or pretending they don't exist.

"I feel like a lot of the answer in Asian culture is just more discipline, more discipline…. Sometimes that can be good, but a lot of times it can look like denying a sensitive connection to yourself and a … kindness to yourself."
He tells The Assembly he now realizes ADHD isn't something he can fix simply by trying harder.

While he has taken medication for the condition before, he says he and his mother were initially reluctant. He then reveals he recently considered trying medication again, but "the Korean in me is like, 'Don't. Just focus, just don't do it. Just work harder.'"

Williams says he got goosebumps when some of the interviewers in The Assembly performed an a cappella version of All the Things She Said by t.A.T.u. — one of the songs included on the Heated Rivalry soundtrack. (CBC/Small Army Entertainment)
The episode ends with Williams sharing the Heated Rivalry message he hopes comes across most clearly:
"You deserve the best love story and the best romance story in your life — no matter who you are."
The episode is full of tender moments, and there are more to be seen in the longer producer's cut now streaming on Gem.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Helen Surgenor is a producer for CBC News based in Toronto, currently working for the entertainment unit. She spent years waking up before dawn to make the daily news podcast World Report. She has reported in Alberta, Iqaluit and Barbados. You can reach her at helen.surgenor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Economic frustration set to boil over in midterm elections
articles.summary: The U.S. economy is booming. But American consumers have never been more pessimistic. Economists blame tariffs and the war with Iran.

image.caption: U.S. President Donald Trump dances during a campaign rally at Rock Hill Sports and Event Center, on Thursday, in Rock Hill, S.C. (Scott Kinser/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Business·Analysis
The U.S. economy is booming. But American consumers have never been more pessimistic. Economists blame tariffs and the war with Iran.
Consumer sentiment hits all-time low as Americans head to the polls
American voters are headed to the polls for the U.S. midterms this week. Most are angry and frustrated about the state of the economy and the way Donald Trump has managed it.
If you want evidence of that dissatisfaction look no further than the University of Michigan's Index of Consumer Sentiment.
It shows consumer confidence is plummetting under Trump.

"Only three times since the 1970s have more than half of Americans said their government's doing bad job managing the economy. Right now it's at 74 per cent," said Kathryn Anne Edwards, a labour economist and policy consultant in Houston.
The index gauges consumer sentiment. It is lower today than it was during the toughest recessions in the 1980s or even the financial crisis in 2008-09.
And she says that survey is one of the biggest and longest standing bodies of economic data in the country. It's been going on since the 1940s. And it's been a monthly survey since 1978.
Edwards says these kinds of numbers show that on some fundamental level, the U.S. economy is failing American households.
"It's so completely unprecedented. It's really hard to put into words," said Edwards.
Those kind of plunges in consumer sentiment historically only happen in the deepest and darkest days of a recession.
And that's what's odd.
The U.S. economy is nowhere near a recession.
The latest GDP numbers out of Washington show the U.S. economy is the fastest growing economy in the Western world.
American GDP expanded by 3.8 per cent in the quarter running from July to September. (By comparison, Canada is on track for about a third of that growth.)
Retail sales were up. Investment in AI continues to churn ever higher. And stock markets are at an all-time high.

"GDP is growing above trend, consumer spending remains robust, layoffs trudge along at ultra-low levels, and we've seen a stable unemployment rate over the past year," wrote RBC's team of economists Mike Reid, Carrie Freestone and Imri Haggin.
But if the macro data is so good, why are voters so angry?

"For many voters, the economy is now synonymous with inflation, as rising prices outweigh job reports, housing affordability and stock market performance," wrote Francis Généreux, lead economist at Desjardins Group in a note to clients.
And those rising prices have been driven by two main things; tariffs and the U.S.-led war with Iran.

Gas prices shot up the day the war began. They have bounced around a little as talk of various ceasefires and deals come and go, but American drivers are paying far more at the pumps today than they were a year ago.
And gasoline prices are posted everywhere as drivers and pedestrians alike move through a neighbourhood. So even if you ride a bicycle to work, the increase in prices is incredibly hard to ignore.
Inflation in the U.S. has ticked up to 3.7 per cent, and economists warn it's not done climbing yet.
Yes, much of that increase is due to energy costs. But tariffs have contributed as well.
A recent report from the New York Federal Reserve found the cost of many everyday items would have declined last year were it not for Trump's tariffs.
Researchers looked at the 12-month change in consumer goods prices going back to the peak of the COVID-era surge in inflation. They showed price growth was still falling in 2024 and reversed in 2025.

"Our estimates attribute this increase to the tariffs: by February 2026, tariffs had contributed 2.9 percentage points to goods price inflation, and without them goods prices would have fallen slightly," wrote Mary Amiti, Sebastian Heise and David E. Weinstein.

And Edwards says voters have followed the Trump administration's policy decisions and how they drive prices. She says there are two sharp drops in the consumer sentiment index. One when tariffs were introduced and the other when the war with Iran began.
"Americans get it. Tariffs have made their lives more expensive," she said.

And Americans will take that knowledge into the polling booth this week. If the polls hold, the midterms could lead to sweeping changes in the formation of Congress and who holds power on Capitol Hill.
But whether those newly elected Senate and House members actually take action to lower tariffs for Canadians is a different question altogether.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Armstrong is the CBC's senior business correspondent. He was a foreign correspondent and a parliamentary reporter for CBC News. Peter hosted the business program On the Money and World Report on CBC Radio. He is the author of the CBC newsletter Mind Your Business

articles.title: Her neighbour built a garden suite. She calls it a 'watchtower' over her Toronto back yard
articles.summary: Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.

image.caption: Sandy Chambers says this past summer she returned from a vacation to find a two-story building looming over her back fence. (Michael Smee/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto
Fed up with what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy, an East York woman is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey.
East York homeowner calls for limit for garden suites to be 1 storey high
An East York homeowner is going public with her campaign to have new garden suites limited to just one storey after what she calls a violation of her backyard privacy.

Sandy Chambers, who lives in the Danforth-Greenwood area, says this past summer she returned from a one-week vacation to find a six-metre-high, two-story building with a picture window, looming over her back fence.
"After you get past the shock there's a little bit of anger," she said. "I lost all privacy in my yard, I stopped using my yard."
"It fired me up."
In response, she planted trees across the back of her yard, and erected a large screen on a backyard shed, which blocks the view from the neighbours’ new picture window.
In 2022, the updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. (Michael Smee/CBC)

She also ordered dozens of lawn signs that read "Save Our Neighbourhoods. No 2-storey Garden Suites Without a Say." An online petition that she started also appears to be gaining traction, she says, so far garnering about 80 signatures.
CBC Toronto tried to speak with the homeowners but no one answered a knock at the door Thursday.
One of the people who is displaying one of those signs on her front lawn is Rosanna Manarin, who lives next door to the house that installed the garden suite.
She says she was shocked at how completely her light and privacy were limited by the new build.
"I understand the city’s need for density, but what is now sitting next door to me is a watchtower," she told CBC Toronto.
Rosanna Manarin, who has lived in the same house for 25 years, says the emergence of a two-storey garden suite overshadowing her yard this past summer was a shock. (Michael Smee/CBC)
“Your oasis is completely gone.”

As much as the neighbours may dislike the new structure, both Chambers and Manarin agree that the homeowners are well within their rights, under new city rules that govern the construction of garden suites.
New planning rules introduced to ease housing issues
Technically, the homeowners are within their rights under new city rules that govern the construction of garden suites.
Garden suites are self-contained, detached units often built in backyards and not connected to a public lane, according to the city of Toronto's website.

In 2022, the city updated planning rules to allow homeowners to build garden suites on their properties with fewer city restrictions. The idea, known as gentle infill housing, was first floated as a way to help ease the city’s housing crunch.

Instead of looking for a zoning change — which would have meant an opportunity for public discussion about the new build — property owners are now only required to apply for a building permit to put up structures such as garden suites and multiplexes.

items: This couple says they are paying the price of Toronto's housing push

blocks.text: The new process doesn't include an opportunity for public input, as long as the plan doesn’t require any variances — smaller setbacks, for instance.

Numbers from the city show the public has reacted enthusiastically. In 2022, the first year that garden suites were allowed without expensive and time-consuming rezoning applications, just 34 building permits were issued. By 2025, that number had risen to a total of 361.
Staff say so far, 627 have been built while another 755 are under construction.
But there have also been complaints.
Garden suites a 'turn off' for buyers: real estate broker
The city does not track criticisms for the initiative, but anecdotally, real estate experts say they’re hearing from unhappy homeowners.
Real estate broker Justin Bregman says potential buyers he’s encountered are not enthusiastic about the lack of light and privacy that some garden suites bring to a neighbourhood.
In terms of resale value, "It’s a turn off," he says.
"If all of a sudden there’s a two-storey, or a 20-foot (six-metre) high [building] that’s completely blocking your backyard, that absolutely is going to affect value."
City staff did not answer directly when asked to comment on Chambers’ drive to have garden suites limited to one storey.

In an email to CBC Toronto, staff wrote: "The City of Toronto recognizes that new construction can raise concerns for neighbouring property owners, including concerns related to privacy, sunlight and construction impacts," the email states.
"While these concerns are understandable…these concerns do not, on their own, provide a basis to withhold a building permit" if the project complies with the provincial building code.

items: Alberta government to force Edmonton to change infill rules

blocks.text: Toronto real estate lawyer Bob Aaron points out that backyard privacy is never guaranteed in an urban neighbourhood.
Garden suites aside, most people with a two storey house can see into a neighbour’s yard.
"Frankly there is no right to privacy from neighbouring properties looking into your property in Canadian law," he said.
"That’s the joy of urban living."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
michael.smee@cbc.ca

articles.title: Commonwealth secretary-general pitches group as 'alternative' to U.S. trade
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for closer diplomatic co-operation between middle powers heads to a new venue this week, as he departs later Monday for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government…

image.caption: Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey attends a reception to mark International Women's Day at St James's Palace, London, Britain, March 10, 2026. (Aaron Chown/Reuters)

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s push for closer diplomatic co-operation between middle powers heads to a new venue this week, as he departs later Monday for the biennial Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting, hosted this year by Antigua and Barbuda.
The timing for this year's talks is extraordinary.

As King Charles, in his ceremonial role as head of the Commonwealth, presides over opening ceremonies and hosts official lunch and dinner events with Commonwealth leaders Tuesday, American voters will be casting their verdict on the Trump administration's increasingly volatile trade and foreign policy agenda.

In her only interview with a Canadian media outlet amid final preparations for the summit in the country's capital, St. John's, Commonwealth Secretary General Shirley Botchwey told CBC News that in this time of global fracture, when global trade is being undermined and the multilateral system is under strain, Commonwealth members are now looking for partnerships they can trust.
"We woke up one day and every one of our 56 countries had been slapped with tariffs," she said. "This is so important, that we look within and enhance and deepen intra-Commonwealth trade."
Carney's attendance, she said, "sends a very powerful signal," casting a "vote of confidence" in the Commonwealth's investment agenda and its potential to become a trading bloc.
Carney should see Commonwealth as trade opportunity: secretary-general

Canadian government officials briefing reporters prior to departure said the Commonwealth's diversity and geographic reach make it a valuable forum for Canada to "build strategic autonomy" by collaborating on issues relevant to its prosperity and security.
They also noted that the Commonwealth includes some of the fastest-growing economies in the world — and as its second-largest financial contributor, Canada plays an influential leadership role.

items: Carney says, unequivocally, Canada seeking to become the EU's 1st associate member

blocks.text: Canada is contributing to the secretariat's renewal and reform, the officials said, by promoting a strong economic agenda at this year's gathering. Canada already does about $100 billion in trade annually with Commonwealth partners, they said, with imports, exports and foreign direct investment all on the rise.

In total, Botchwey said, Commonwealth partners do about $900 billion worth of trade with each other. By the time leaders meet again, she said, her secretariat's goal is to more than double it, to $2 trillion.
Removing trade barriers between Commonwealth members, she suggested, dovetails nicely with the Carney government's attempt to be less reliant on trade with the United States.
PM not attending entire summit

Carney, however, is not attending the entire summit, which began on Sunday and runs through Wednesday. After a full day of ceremonial events, deliberations and networking on Tuesday, he's expected to return to Ottawa, amid preparations for Thursday's federal budget.

Not every head of government is expected to attend this year. New Zealand is in the throes of an election campaign. Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi rarely travels to attend summits like this one and hasn't joined a Commonwealth gathering since 2018. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has also skipped the last two.
However, Botchwey is expecting about 30 leaders to make the trip to Antigua — a good turnout, by her estimation, and a hopeful sign of the summit's relevance in challenging times.
Canada and EU launching 'alliance for the future,' Carney says

Carney's many travels since becoming prime minister have yet to see him touch down in the Caribbean. To nurture diplomatic relationships in this part of the world, a breakfast meeting with regional leaders is one of the first things on his itinerary in Antigua on Tuesday morning, Canadian officials told reporters.

Unlike the other summits on Carney's dance card later this month across Asia — the Francophonie Summit hosted by Cambodia, ASEAN (Southeast Asian countries) in the Philippines and APEC (the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum) in Shenzhen, China — the 56 member countries represented at the Commonwealth summit have all committed to a Charter that upholds human rights and democratic governance.

English is a common language across all their business communities, and while each enforces its own regulations, Commonwealth countries generally have comparable legal systems. All have committed to principles like gender equality, environmental protection and sustainable development.

items: Far right gains ground in Europe as Canada pivots from Trump to EU

blocks.text: This summit hopes to turn those common values into a comparative economic advantage.

"We know that [Carney] has made a lot of strides in terms of moving close to Europe, [and] also for the middle powers to come together in terms of having their voice heard," Botchwey said. "His being here gives him an opportunity to now look at the countries in the Commonwealth as an opportunity for trade, an opportunity for dialogue."

Commonwealth partners offer a combined market of 2.7 billion people, she noted, 1.6 billion of whom are young people under 30. "I think that it is extremely important that he sees it as an alternative [to the U.S.]"
Private sector also taking part

Business leaders pitching new ventures will be able to network directly with Commonwealth trading partners at several events this week, including a private breakfast on Wednesday morning to kick off the leaders' retreat on Jumby Bay Island, an exclusive resort just off Antigua's northeast coast.

Last month, the Commonwealth secretariat launched a new investment platform, which is now populated online with dozens of "bankable" infrastructure, resource development and other private and public sector projects around the world, seeking tens of billions in financing.

While many of the projects listed so far are in African and Caribbean member countries, Botchwey said this isn't simply a one-way conversation designed to lean on wealthier donor countries like Canada.
Beachgoers are silhouetted against the setting sun ahead of the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Runaway Bay, Antigua and Barbuda, on Saturday. (Matias Delacroix/The Associated)
"It's a two-way stream. It cannot be one-way, where developing countries are seeking investment only," she said. "We are so fortunate to have a mix [of big and small countries.]"
Botchwey identified critical minerals projects as something Carney could want to discuss with Commonwealth partners in Africa as well as Australia.
Are any deals ready to announce?
"Yes, yes. I look forward to some big deals happening," she said. "At least, the start of these deals happening."
As these potential new partnerships take off, the results of the U.S. midterms will be landing.
"I'm sure many of the heads [of government] will be paying attention to that as well," the secretary general said with a smile. "We all will."

articles.title: Ukraine and Russia say emergency air-raid warning systems hit by cyber-hacks – Europe live
articles.summary:
In Ukraine, the app started to send out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.

Ukraine and Russia have…

blocks.text: Key events

items: 30m agoOpening summary

blocks.text: Opening summary
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of key events in Europe.
Ukraine and Russia have reported corresponding cyber-hacks on their app warning systems overnight.
These are the mobile apps which send alerts and air-raid warnings, alerting citizens to when missiles and drones are incoming (and thus advising residents to seek shelter or go down to a bunker).

This appears to be the first breach of the app, on such a scale, during the war so far; directly immobilising one of the most important channels of communication authorities have to help advise citizens.

In the Ukraine hack, the app started spewing out alarming fake messages late on Sunday night – warning residents of a nuclear radiation threat in the capital Kyiv, a chemical attack, street fighting and also incoming Oreshnik hypersonic missiles, which Ukraine lacks interceptors for.
Ukraine’s Air Force issued clarification within the hour on Telegram, urging people to remain calm and disregard the messages, one of which was written in Russian.

Some hours later, Russian authorities said its warning app had been hacked and had to be taken offline. A Ukrainian hacker group has claimed to have sent fake alerts warning of nuclear warheads to users inside Russia.
Amid the cyber warfare overnight, both sides also carried out strikes, targeting energy sites like oil refineries. Strikes have been reported in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa.
Stay with us for all the developments.

articles.title: For US Democrats, climate policy is now about energy bills
articles.summary: 'Climate change' has nearly vanished from many Democrats' campaign pitch, replaced by electricity prices. What would the party actually do on climate if it won the midterms?

image.caption: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico has pitched voters on lower energy bills rather than fighting climate changeImage: Abigail Dollins/Fort Worth Star-Telegram/TNS/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: President Donald Trump's administration has gutted US climate policy. Yet even as wildfires, record heat waves and flooding hit communities across the country, Democrats are keeping quiet about global warming on the midterm campaign trail.

Instead, candidates are packaging climate policy as an affordability issue, stressing how Americans are struggling to afford gas, groceries and to insure their homes against climate-fueled weather extremes.

Take Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico in Texas, who represents the party's best chance at winning the race in the Republican stronghold in nearly 40 years. Though he makes some mention of climate change on his campaign's "energy and environment" page, that is not his focus.
His pledges center around lowering energy costs, providing emergency relief for spiking utility bills, making data centers pay for their own grid upgrades and growing energy sector jobs.

This aligns with analysis from nonprofit news organization Inside Climate News showing that the Democrats have dramatically reduced mentions of climate change in their press releases and campaign messaging.

blocks.caption: The Trump administration has pushed back against renewables in favor of fossil fuels, but rooftop solar is gaining popularity with US homeownersImage: Mario Tama/Getty Images

blocks.text: "We've entered an interesting space where climate policy doesn't need to be called climate policy to be climate policy," Max Frankel, executive director of the SEEC Institute, a nonprofit that helps guide climate policy in Congress, told DW.
What would a Democratic win mean for climate policy?

Most forecasts project Democrats winning the House and a narrow majority in the Senate in the November 3 election. But without control of the White House, passing any legislation will be difficult and almost any climate policy will have to be a bipartisan endeavor, say analysts.

Given that and the Democrats shift to affordability over climate, few experts expect a fully resurrected Inflation Reduction Act. Introduced under the Democrats to create incentives for building clean energy projects, the legislation was largely decimated by President Trump's major tax law.

But Democrats may try to bring back some climate-friendly IRA provisions, particularly measures aimed at lowering household energy costs, analysts told DW. Those include incentives for home energy-efficiency upgrades and appliances like heat pumps to replace oil and gas heaters that typically help bring down household energy bills.

Politicians could also expand an IRA manufacturing tax credit for solar, batteries, and critical minerals that largely survived. One bipartisan bill proposes extending it to include nuclear fusion components.

"It's not going to be anything at the scale of the IRA," Adrian Deveny, founder of Climate Vision, a policy firm dedicated to decarbonization, told DW. "It's like singles and doubles as opposed to a home run, which is still worth doing."
A first bipartisan test over building infrastructure
In a rare area of agreement between the parties, some Democrats and Republicans are already backing a reform bill they're hoping to pass before a new Congress is sworn in January.

If enacted, the bill could make it significantly easier to build major infrastructure projects in the US, including long-distance transmission lines that carry electricity between regions but that currently take years to build because of complex permitting rules.
US turns its back on EVs

"The biggest beneficiary of building more transmission will be wind and solar power, because the best and cheapest way to generate wind and solar energy tends to be far away from cities," said David Spence, a political scientist at the University of Texas who researches the politics of energy regulation. "And so, they need transmission to get their product to market."
But environmental groups say the bill could also speed up the approval of fossil fuel projects.
If Democrats win big in the midterms there might be some "peeling off their support for that bill because they think they can do better in the next Congress," said Spence.
Looking to the 2028 presidential elections

Major new federal climate legislation is a long shot before the 2028 presidential election. And afterwards it would likely require Democrats winning the White House, the Senate and the House. While no 2028 platforms have been released yet, policy experts expect a few ideas to feature prominently.

One is data centers. Opposition to the energy-guzzling infrastructure being built en masse to power the AI boom is mounting across the country. Half of Americans are now against data centers being built close to their homes, according to a pollfrom news outlet Politico.

"I'm sure every candidate is going to have a platform with a focus on data center constraints on some level, as a way to address affordability," Deveny, who led negotiations on the IRA, said. "And that's the entry point for climate policy."

There are several ideas currently circulating — including a proposal by Democrats Bernie Sanders and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to pause data center construction — as well as ending tax breaks for data centers and imposing new taxes on their electricity use.

blocks.caption: Wind energy has taken a hit under President Trump, who has incentivized energy companies to cancel offshore wind leasesImage: Steve Helber/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Democrats may also seek to restore the IRA's clean energy tax incentives. This year, more than 150 legislators co-sponsored the so-called Energy Bills Relief Act designed to reinstate IRA clean energy tax incentives, reform how transmission permits are granted, and make data centers pay for the grid upgrades they need. The bill is unlikely to pass anytime soon but offers a window into what Democrats might support.

"By far, the biggest consensus — to the extent there's anything remotely resembling a consensus — is restoring a lot of the clean energy tax incentives from the IRA," Deveny said. "Not everybody supports that but it is a highly supported idea amongst most congressional Democrats."

Support for other proposals include a new federal program to help insurers cover climate-driven disasters and bring down hefty premiums, as well as so-called climate superfunds. This would require fossil fuel companies to contribute to the costs of damage caused by extreme weather and adapting to the risks of climate change.
Vermont and New York both passed legislation to create funds, although a federal judge blocked New York's.

The 2028 presidential race is expected to begin a few weeks after the midterms end, bringing a fresh round of policy ideas and debates. A new president typically gets to drive the legislative agenda in the beginning of their term if their party also wins Congress.

"As long as the consensus is that clean energy is the cheaper source of energy, and it's going to provide stability over the long term for high energy costs — there's a million ways you can propose solutions through that lens," Deveny said.

articles.title: Uganda begins withdrawing troops from Somalia after 20 years
articles.summary: The country was the first to contribute troops to the AU mission established to stabilise Somalia in 2007.

blocks.text: Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
The first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson, Chris Magezi, did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), which was established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
Last week, Gen Muhoozi said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
The withdrawal is being carried out in phases and is expected to be completed in August 2027.
However, Uganda is not ending its entire military involvement in Somalia. Its troops deployed under a separate bilateral security arrangement will remain in the country.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency led al-Shabab, an al-Qaeda-linked militant group, for more than two decades.
Uganda forces first deployed to the country in 2007 and played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.

Ugandan troops continued its military involvement under successive Africa Union, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.

It was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin to in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

articles.title: Can’t keep up with COP lingo? This list has got you covered
articles.summary: (1st UPDATE) This guide to the UN climate summit's terms and acronyms will help you understand the negotiations shaping the world's efforts to address the climate crisis

blocks.text: This story was first published on November 14, 2025. Due to recent events, we are republishing it with updated information.
If this is your first time tuning in to the United Nations (UN) Climate Change Conference or COP, you might be a little lost.

A meeting among world leaders on solving the climate crisis sounds simple enough. That is, until you throw in a bunch of acronyms like NDCs, NAPs, and GST, along with technical terms like carbon markets, climate debt, and concessional finance — all with an extra side of a whole lot of politics.
As world leaders navigate the two-week-long conference’s complicated landscape, everyone else has to make sense of whatever it is that’s coming out of their mouths.
Here’s a list of terms you need to know if you’re tuning in to COP — which you probably should be doing if you care anything about our warming world.

blocks.caption: Can’t keep up with COP lingo? This list has got you covered

blocks.text: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) – It is a treaty adopted in 1992 to halt climate change. It has since been joined by 198 countries, and is the parent treaty of the 1997 Kyoto Protocol and 2015 Paris Agreement. The ultimate goal of all these agreements is to control greenhouse gas emissions so that we do not end up irrevocably changing our climate to a dangerous degree.

Conference of the Parties (COP) – As a generic term, it refers to the decision-making body composed of the countries who agreed on an international treaty or convention. In the context of the world’s climate agreements, it is an annual summit of countries who signed the UNFCCC, where they decide how to implement their commitments to tackle climate change. During the COP, countries also meet to discuss the Kyoto Protocol and Paris Agreement in conferences known as the CMP and CMA, respectively.

1.5ºC – A tipping point in the Earth’s temperature that triggers irreversible and self-reinforcing changes in the environment, as identified by scientists. These changes include the Amazon rainforest turning into a savanna, melting ice sheets, or dying coral reefs, among others.

35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge – It is a pledge by governments to accelerate the clean energy transition by increasing the share of global final energy consumption met by electricity from almost 24% in 2023 to 35% by 2035.

Action Agenda – A platform for civil society to join voluntary initiatives that will accelerate emissions reduction, boost climate resilience, and support the transition to sustainable economies. It became a part of the COP’s regular program in COP21 back in 2015 as an initiative to expand beyond government negotiations and include people who don’t negotiate during the COP but act to put agreements into practice, like businesses, investors, and local governments.

Adaptation – It refers to preparations made for a warmer world with more heat waves and higher sea levels. They can include strategies like planting trees for shade or safeguarding supplies against extreme weather disruptions. Funding for these strategies is called adaptation finance. (EXPLAINER: A guide to UN climate jargon, from NDCs to ‘unabated’ emissions)

Baku Finance Goal – It is a commitment to channel $1.3 trillion to developing countries each year that will help them implement climate plans. To achieve this goal, developed countries must take the lead in mobilizing at least $300 billion per year for developing countries by 2035. The blueprint to achieve this is called the Baku to Belém Roadmap.

Belem Action Mechanism for a Global Just Transition (BAM) – It is a proposed mechanism that will outline how governments and the private sector can put people at the heart of national and sectoral transitions to renewable energy. This includes job creation, worker training, and strategies to diversify industries into climate planning and investment.

Biennial transparency reports (BTR) – Every two years, countries are required to submit a report on national inventories of their emissions, progress toward their nationally determined contributions, policies and measures, climate change impacts and adaptation, financial and technical support provided or needed, and areas for improvement. The first submission of these reports was in December 2024, which means the second submission period will fall a month after COP31 in 2026 ends.

Carbon credits – The carbon crediting mechanism was established under the Paris Agreement. When countries or companies reduce greenhouse gas emissions, they earn carbon credits that they can sell to other companies. Buying these credits allows companies to comply with their own emissions reduction obligations or meet net-zero targets. The trading systems in which carbon credits are sold and bought are called carbon markets.

Common but differentiated responsibilities (CBDR) – Based on a “polluter pays” principle, this idea says that wealthy countries should do more to rein in climate change because they contributed the most emissions historically to the atmosphere.
Climate debt – It is the sum of damages caused by emissions from developed countries on developing countries who do not emit as much yet are the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

Climate finance – Funding provided by governments, development banks, private investors, and philanthropies to help countries lower greenhouse gas emissions or adapt to climate impacts. These include renewable energy projects or protection from floods, among others. (READ: What is climate finance and why does it matter?)

Champions – A person acting as a liaison between governments and civil society on behalf of the COP president, specifically working to involve businesses, communities, financial institutions, and other actors who do not negotiate climate agreements but are essential for putting them into practice. There are two types: high-level champions and youth champions. Each champion serves a term of two years.

Climate justice – An idea recognizing that those who contribute least to carbon emissions are paying the highest cost. It means holding responsible countries, corporations, and people that drive the climate crisis.

Concessional finance – It refers to below market rate finance provided by major financial institutions, like development banks and multilateral funds, to developing countries to accelerate development or climate objectives.
COP Truce – It is an appeal to nations to stop military operations during the month of the COP.

Cover decision – A statement outlining the high-level political agreements on key issues. It embodies what the summit has achieved and the broad goals that every country has agreed to pursue. (EXPLAINER: What happens at a COP climate summit?)
Decarbonization – The process of reducing carbon emissions.

Global Goal on Adaptation (GGA) – It was established in Article 7 of the Paris Agreement as a goal to enhance a country’s capacity to adapt, strengthen resilience, and reduce vulnerability to climate change. It provides a system for countries to track their adaptation progress and urge them to act on managing climate change risks.

Global Implementation Accelerator (GIA) – It is a “cooperative, facilitative, and voluntary initiative” that aims to speed up programs to keep 1.5°C within reach and support countries in implementing their nationally determined contributions and national adaptation plans. The initiative started at COP30 in 2025 and will continue into COP31. It will focus on specific actions on the ground and the mobilization of all actors.

Global stocktake (GST) – It is a periodical assessment of the collective progress in achieving the Paris Agreement. It takes place every five years, with the first-ever stocktake concluded at COP28 in 2023. This assessment informs the climate action plans of every country.

Green Climate Fund – A fund established under the Paris Agreement to distribute $100 billion in annual climate finance from wealthy nations to help developing countries fund the energy transition and projects for adapting to a warmer world.
High-Level Segment – A part of the COP where national leaders give back-to-back speeches in the venue’s main plenary hall.

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) – It is the UNFCCC’s main scientific body, where scientists from the countries who signed the treaty work together to release reports every six to seven years detailing global scientific consensus on climate science.

Just transition – A shift from fossil fuels, like coal into renewable energy sources, that looks after those who will be displaced by the energy transition, especially workers. (EXPLAINER: What is just energy transition?)

Kyoto Protocol – A treaty that entered into force in 2005 where industrialized countries agreed to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with agreed individual targets. It only binds developed countries, placing a heavier burden on them because they are largely responsible for the high levels of these emissions in the atmosphere.

Loss and Damage Fund – Loss and damage refers to the negative consequences of climate change, like extreme weather events, rising sea levels, prolonged heatwaves, changes in ocean conditions, and damage to agriculture. They still occur despite mitigation and adaptation efforts, so COP28 approved a fund that will provide financial assistance to nations most vulnerable and impacted by these harmful effects. The Philippines is the host of this fund’s board.

Mitigation – It refers to the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions to slow, if not halt, global warming. It is the main focus in the world’s transition away from fossil fuels to renewable energy sources.
Montreal Protocol – It is an international agreement that regulates the production and consumption of nearly 100 man-made chemicals that harm and deplete the ozone layer.

Mutirão Decision – It is the cover decision or final agreement made between countries at the end of COP30 hosted by Brazil. It was a compromise climate deal aimed at boosting finance for poor nations coping with global warming, although it omitted any mention of the fossil fuels driving it. The term “Mutirão” originally comes from the Tupi-Guarani language of Brazil and can be translated as “collective efforts.”

National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) – They are strategies developed by countries, particularly developing nations, to prepare for and respond to the impacts of climate change, such as droughts, floods, and sea level rise. Their main goals are to reduce climate vulnerability, integrate adaptation into public policies, plan actions based on scientific data, and access international climate finance.

Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) – These are pledges by each country on their target amount for reducing greenhouse gas emissions and their plans to adapt to the impacts of climate change. They are submitted every five years to the UNFCCC secretariat, and must represent a progression compared to the previous NDC, reflecting a country’s highest possible ambition.
Net zero – It means releasing no more emissions than can be recaptured by technology, tree-planting, or other means. In short, reaching net zero means greenhouse gas concentrations stop increasing.

Negotiating group – Countries sending delegations are distributed into groups or blocs that work together to represent their common interests in international climate change negotiations. The Philippines is part of the Group of 77 + China — the largest alliance of developing countries that promotes the interests of the Global South — and co-founded (but eventually left) the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc.

New Collective Quantified Goal (NCQG) – It is a global climate finance goal set from a floor of $100 billion per year. In COP29 in 2024, they came up with a $300-billion annual target, called the Baku Finance Goal.

Paris Agreement – A legally binding international treaty enacted in 2016 that aims to keep the increase in global average temperature to 2ºC — but preferably 1.5ºC — above levels before the Industrial Revolution. Under the agreement, signatory countries are expected to present their action plan to align with these goals. It also provides a framework for developing countries to receive support from developed countries. (READ: Where are we now on the Paris Agreement, a decade after it was adopted?)

Paris Rulebook – These are the implementation guidelines for the Paris Agreement, laying out the tools and processes for them to fully, fairly, and effectively follow the climate plans outlined in their NDCs. It was completed in COP29.
Phaseout – A gradual reduction in the production and use of fossil fuels.

Santa Marta First Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels (TAFF) – After COP30 omitted a fossil fuel phaseout in its final decision, this conference was held in Colombia in April 2026 and convened a 57-country “coalition of the willing” (excluding China, Russia, the US, and India to prevent the same deadlock that occurred in the previous year’s climate summit). The conference established a voluntary TAFF coordination process and adopted the “Santa Marta Vision” meant to inform the COP31 global fossil fuel roadmap.

Secretariat – The UNFCCC secretariat, also referred to as UN Climate Change, is the UN entity tasked with supporting the world’s response to climate change. It organizes and supports the COP and other negotiations, provides technical expertise and reviews climate change information reported in these negotiations, and maintains a registry for NDCs.

Small Island Developing States (SIDS) – They are a distinct group of 39 states and 18 associate members of UN regional commissions located in the Caribbean, the Pacific, and the Atlantic, Indian Ocean and South China Sea. They face unique social, economic, and environmental vulnerabilities because of their remote geography, such as high import and export costs for goods, irregular international traffic volumes, and a narrow resource base.

The Troika – The host countries of COP28, COP29, and COP30, who said they were collaborating to ensure continuity in organizing the annual UN climate talks. All three countries have economies that rely on fossil fuels.
Tropical Forests Forever Facility (TFFF) – It is a global fund supporting tropical forest conservation that was first announced during COP30.

UAE Consensus – It is a response to the results of the first global stocktake, setting standards for a just transition and goals like tripling renewable energy, halting deforestation, and doubling energy efficiency by 2030.
Unabated emissions – Describes carbon pollution not being captured by new technologies such as carbon capture and storage. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Published November 2, 2026 4:35pm

The International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber III is set to hold its fifth and final status conference on Monday for the case against former President Rodrigo Roa Duterte, ahead of the start of his trial proper on November 30, 2026.
During the status conference, the court is expected to discuss key procedural preparations for the upcoming trial.
The session is scheduled to run from 10 a.m. to 11:30 a.m. (5 p.m. to 6:30 p.m. Philippine time), with an additional session set from 12 p.m. to 1:30 p.m. (7 p.m. to 8:30 p.m.), if needed.
The hearing will be broadcast on a 30-minute delay via the ICC’s official website and social media accounts.
For this final status conference, Trial Chamber III and the parties are expected to tackle the following:

items: Daily sitting schedule
Audio-Visual Link testimony and Rights of Audience
List of Witnesses
Number of hours for the Prosecution's presentation of evidence
Potentially Exculpatory Evidence, agreed facts and calling order
Rule 68(3) applications and in-court protective measures
Security of Defence missions

blocks.text: According to a document released Friday, Duterte will not attend the fifth status conference after being granted leave by Trial Chamber III. He will instead be represented by his lawyers. —LDF, GMA News

blocks.text: Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff to pay for a sharp rise in its fuel costs which have surged following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The carrier said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.

articles.title: Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
articles.summary: The author of Jasper Jones and Runt pleaded guilty in May after police raided his home months earlier.

blocks.text: Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".

In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.

She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.

"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.

Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

articles.title: Award‑winning Australian children’s author Craig Silvey jailed over child exploitation material
articles.summary:
Jasper Jones writer sent multiple messages about his sexual desire for young boys, Western Australian district court hears

  • Warning:…

blocks.text: The award‑winning author Craig Silvey sent multiple messages about his sexual desire for young boys and was caught with explicit images of children and adults.
The young adult novelist was jailed on Monday for seven months after pleading guilty to distributing and possessing child exploitation material earlier this year.
The 44-year-old was found with numerous category one photos and videos on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his Fremantle home, the Western Australian district court heard.
Silvey, a father of three, also engaged in an online conversation with another user on a pornography website, where his handle was Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy.
In the chat, Silvey described himself as a “Fremantle guy” before telling the user: “You sound amazing … we have very similar interests, would love to chat more; do you have Signal or Session?”
The pair moved to an encrypted messaging app, where he said he was “extremely open-minded and obsessed with taboos” and preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.

Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the International Dublin Literary Award, also wrote he was “drooling” over a sexually explicit photo of a naked man and boy together.
Judge Hayley Cormann said it was very serious and very disturbing offending.
“This offending involves children and it is destructive and it is devastating,” she said.
The popular author is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, considered a modern Australian classic and adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
after newsletter promotion
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.
Publishers Allen & Unwin and Fremantle Press, which released Rhubarb, stopped promoting his books after Silvey was charged and most of his titles were removed from reading lists across the country.
Two charges of producing and possessing further child exploitation material were dropped in May.

articles.title: US: Nine killed in Florida jet crash
articles.summary: A Learjet plane crashed near a busy road in a residential neighborhood in Palm Beach County, leaving all nine people on board dead and a large crater on ground.

image.caption: The cause of the crash and the identities of those on board the plane were not immediately knownImage: Chris Beckett/ZUMA/IMAGO

blocks.text: A private jet crashed in a residential area of Cresthaven in the US state of Florida's Palm Beach County on Sunday, killing all nine people on board.
The Learjet 60 business jet nose-dived into the south Florida neighborhood and exploded.

Videos circulating on social media, recorded by people from their vehicles, shows the plane making a loud whooshing sound as it rapidly descends to hit the side of a road and erupts into a large fireball.
The plane's descent in the footage resembled — as Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described — "a missile going down."
A thick plume of black and gray smoke is seen rising against houses, which were narrowly missed.
The crash left a crater on the road, with flames flickering around it.
What do we know about the Florida plane crash?
The plane had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International ⁠Airport in Texas and was bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
It was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 10,660 meters) when the pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation. They requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).

Just moments after, the jet dived steeply, at 10,000 feet per minute initially and then at 20,000 feet per minute to reach up to 30,000 feet per minute — a speed exceeding the plane's design limits — as per air traffic control recording and flight tracking data.
Last words from the cockpit — 'We are out of time'
LiveATC, which provides live air traffic control broadcasts, captured the harrowing final moments of the crash in an audio recording from a Miami air traffic control center.
A person from the plane's cockpit is heard saying "Mayday, mayday, we are descending 10,000 feet per minute."
The person declares an "emergency" just seconds later, urgently reporting a descent of 20,000 feet per minute.
"We're going to crash into ⁠the ground" the voice from the cockpit says and then goes on to report that the descent was at 22,000 feet and the plane was banking 60 degrees.
A scream is heard before the final words from the cockpit — "We are out of time."
Investigation underway
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said that the crash occurred at 12.50 pm local time and described the incident as a "horrific tragedy."
The cause of the crash and the identities of those on board the plane were not immediately known.
The National Transportation Safety Board has launched a probe into the incident.
There are no immediate reports of anyone on the ground being injured or killed.
Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a press briefing that some 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two ​shelters.
